en: The Third Chapter.
Now, what is this "rasa" (aesthetic flavor)? It is said:
[Vijñapriyā:]
(vi, ka) Since it has been stated that "speech has rasa as its soul," he asks [the following] in order to define *rasa*: "Now" (*atha*).
*Locanā*:
(lo, a) Desiring to define the essential nature of *rasa*, he says "Now" (*atha*), demonstrating that it has reached its proper occasion.
Now—after the definition of the nature of poetry—the meaning is: "What is this *rasa*, of which the sentence constitutes the essence of poetry? In response to this inquiry, its nature is described:
"Manifested by the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and likewise the transitory states (*saṃcārī*)."
Vijñapriyā:
(b) *vibhāva* consists of the two types of causes—the objective (*ālambana*) and the excitant (*uddīpana*)—of love and the other [rasas];
*anubhāva* is its effect.
The *sañcārī* is the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārī*), which consists of specific effects such as despondency (*nirveda*) and the like.
Its separate mention follows the analogy of the "bull among cows" (*govṛṣanyāya*), for the purpose of emphasizing its excellence.
And [the excellence] of *rasa* and the like [is established] because it is quickly communicated.

Although it will be stated that the three factors—the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth—must be combined to constitute the cause of *rasa*, nevertheless, in a verse where they are not all present together, when one [factor] manifests another [factor], the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are manifested more quickly than by depending on others; through this means, *rasa* itself is also quickly communicated.
The object of awakening—the stable emotion such as love and so forth—attains the state of aesthetic flavor (rasa) for those possessed of consciousness. (VisSd 3.1)
Vijñapriyā: (ga) The syntactical connection is that the stable emotion (*sthāyībhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and so forth, attains the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that love and other emotions occurring in characters such as Rāma are manifested by the determinants (*vibhāva*) and the rest?"
It is precisely due to the manifestation of those [factors] that the designation "suggestive of an imperceptible sequence" (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) applies to rasa and the like.

Consequently, that [emotion] such as love (*rati*), brought forth by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is superimposed—through the operation called "tasting" (*svādana*) residing in the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so on—non-differently from the love of the spectator; thus, by virtue of its nature as self-luminous bliss, it transforms accordingly, and in this way, it attains the status of *rasa* within the spectator.
In this very way, its manifestation will occur later.
*Locanā*:
Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of *vibhāva*," for those who possess consciousness—that is, for sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*)—the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is love and so forth.
By the etymological derivation *bhāvyate* (is cultivated) or *vāsyate* (is perfumed), the meaning is that which is latent within beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*).
As it has been said:
"This predisposition, existing since beginningless time, resides in the hearts of sentient beings."
Having encountered its own causal complex, it becomes manifest and attains the nature of rasa.

Although in this context rasa is of an undivided nature, being relished like the taste of a blended beverage (prapānaka) wherein the erotic and other emotions are combined, nevertheless, by conforming to worldly convention and through recognition, the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) attains the state of rasa.
The excitants (vibhāvas) and so forth will be explained later.
Locanā:
He explains what was stated [in the verse] by the words "vibhāvādayaḥ" (the excitants, etc.):
it will be explained right here in this same chapter.
In general, however:
"If those causes, effects,
and auxiliary factors of the stable emotion (sthāyin) such as love that exist in the world are present in drama and poetry,"
The determinants (vibhāvas) and the consequents (anubhāvas), as well as the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas), are now described.
These are the types mentioned.
By Daṇḍin and others it is stated:
"By means of the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary states (sāttvikas), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhis)..."
"The stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), having been brought [to the spectator] and led to a state of being relished, is known as rasa."
The *sāttvika* states are not mentioned separately because they take the form of *anubhāvas*.
[Vijñapriyā] (vi, gha):
But surely the *sāttvika* state also manifests rasa and the like?
Why is he not mentioned? To this he says: "and the *sāttvika* [emotions].
These will be explained further on. (Locanā)
(Lo, ī) Having raised the objection, "How is it that the *sāttvika* [emotions] are not included in this definition?", he says: "And the *sāttvika*s.
The *sāttvika*s are paralysis, perspiration, and so forth.

Rasa is manifested (*vyakta*)—transformed into another form according to the analogy of curd and the like—and thus made manifest; it is not, however, manifested as something already established beforehand, like a jar by means of a lamp.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) He demonstrates the established doctrine of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) with the phrase "by the analogy of milk and so forth":
just as milk itself transforms into the form of curds and the like through contact with an acidic substance; [so too does consciousness transform].

By that same principle, the meaning is as follows: the love (rati) of Rāma and others, being superimposed through non-difference upon the love of the spectators by means of the operation called "savoring" (svādana) residing in the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, transforms into a state of knowledge consisting of self-luminous bliss.
Having shown the meaning of the word "manifested" (vyakta) by the phrase ending with "transformed" (pariṇata), [the author states] that rasa is precisely in such a state.
Demonstrating that it is not, however, in such a state [as ordinary passion], he says again: "Manifested" (*vyakta*) means precisely "made manifest" (*vyaktīkṛta*).

And this will be explained later as "manifestation" (*vyakti*): namely, the making an object of the spectator's own passion and so forth—which is of the nature of self-luminous bliss—by means of a further operation called the "tasting of the manifested rasa," which is non-different from the operation of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) and resides in the *vibhāvas* and other factors, and which consists in the superimposition of Rāma’s passion and so forth.
Locanā:
"(Lo, u) *dadhyādi* means—as for example, milk transforms into the form of curds; this is the meaning.
Thus it has been stated by the authors of the *Locana*:"
"The statement, 'The tastes are perceived,' is a conventional expression, like saying 'He cooks the rice.
Vijñapriyā:
"Like saying 'He cooks the rice'."

The meaning is as follows: just as the term "cooking of rice" (*taṇḍulapāka*) is applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) to the production of cooked rice (*odana*) immediately following the cooking process by way of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), so too is there a metaphorical application of the term "suggestion" (*pratīti*) to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by way of suggestion.
This metaphorical usage is purely mental.
But this is not a verbal metaphor;
rather, it should be understood that there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "rice" (*odana*) for the grain (*taṇḍula*).
*Locanā*:
Just as in the expression "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), the rice is certainly not something already established that is merely manifested;
rather, it becomes rice only when it has been cooked. Similarly, the meaning here is that this [sentiment] also becomes a rasa only when it is manifested.

Furthermore, although the status of being a *sthāyin* (permanent emotion) is already implied by the mention of the terms "love" (*rati*) and so forth, the explicit mention of the term *sthāyin* again is for the purpose of establishing that love and the other emotions can also serve as *sthāyins* within different rasas.
Consequently, laughter, anger, and the like are merely transitory states (vyabhicārin) within the erotic, heroic, and other rasas.
As it has been said:
"A fundamental emotion (bhāva), when it reaches the state of rasa, attains the status of a permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva)."
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding what was stated—that "love and so forth become rasa for those with sensitivity"—he states the purpose of employing the term "sthāyin" therein: "here, 'love and so forth'...
It should be understood that this is not intended to establish their non-permanence (*asthāyitva*), but rather to establish their status as transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
He says this with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*).
He provides corroboration regarding the absence of stability in other *rasas* with the statement: "It has been said: 'in the state of *rasa*' (*rasāvastha*)";
that is, for which *rasa* itself is the subsequent state (*avasthā*).

The meaning is that only such states as laughter, anger, and so forth attain the status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*); however, those in a state other than such [transient] conditions do not attain the status of a permanent emotion. — *Locanā*
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "anger and so forth," [emotions] such as disgust (*jugupsā*) are included.
"Existing in the state of rasa" (*rasāvasthaḥ*) means being fit for attaining the nature of rasa.
The manner of its aesthetic relish (*āsvādana*) is now described, which contains within it an exposition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Through the predominance of *sattva*, it consists of consciousness that is indivisible, self-luminous bliss, devoid of contact with any other object of knowledge, and born of the same womb as the savor of Brahman. (VisSd 3.2)
Vijñapriyā:
He himself will explain the meaning of the verse, "due to the abundance of *sattva*," word by word.
Regarding the term *cinmaya*, *cit* means knowledge (*jñāna*).

"Like its own form, as non-different"—this means that this *rasa*, which consists of the cognition of love (*rati*) and so forth, is tasted as qualified by non-difference from love and the rest, by virtue of its transformation (*pariṇāma*). However, non-difference is not a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition thereof.

This is because *rasa* is precisely that self-luminous tasting (*āsvāda*) of the love and so forth belonging to the spectator—the substratum—which is [tasted] as non-different from the love and so forth of Rāma and others who are being superimposed; and in that [tasting], there is an absence of non-difference.

In that regard, since there is no difference between the relish [of an object] and the pleasure directed toward its object, he provides an example for the theory of the self-form (*svākāravāda*) by stating "like its own form" (*svākāravat*).
For in the theory of the self-form, the object is non-different from the cognition; it is simply the form of the cognition itself.
— *Locanā*

(La, ṝ) Anticipating the question, "What kind of this [rasa] is now being attained, such that people, greedy for its savoring, will engage in poetry?", he introduces the verse beginning with "sattvodrekāt" by stating:
"of this" (*asya*) refers to the manner of savoring (*āsvādana-prakāra*); this is a figurative usage (*upacāra-prayoga*), because this [rasa] is distinct from mere savoring.
"Due to the predominance of *sattva*"—the form is one's own self (*svātman*). The ellipsis is that it is experienced as non-different; in that manner, this [self] is tasted.
He explains:
This aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose life-force is the wondrousness of the supramundane, is relished by certain subjects as if it were non-different from their own mental forms.

"Sattva is said here to be the mind untouched by rajas and tamas"—according to this stated definition, *sattva* is a certain internal quality that brings about an aversion toward external objects of cognition.
Its "predominance" (*udreka*) is its manifestation after having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*.
And the cause for this is the cultivation of such extraordinary and supramundane objects.

It is "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*), meaning this [experience] is a single unity consisting of the aesthetic wonder of bliss arising from the manifestation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, such as love (*rati*) and the like; we shall state the reason for this later.
Its "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*) and other qualities will also be explained according to the logic to be presented.
In the term *cinmaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) "By means of rajas and tamas"—for the mind (*manas*) consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), being composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
External objects of cognition (*meyāḥ*) are such things as jars and cloths.
The internal reality (*dharma*) consists in the state of abiding as pure being (*sattva*) alone.

Now, one might ask: "How does such an intensification of *sattva* arise, and consequently, how can there be awakening from that [state] which is indivisible, self-luminous bliss? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And therein... (*tatra ca*).

This is the intended meaning: from the words of the Blessed One, “O Bhārata, *sattva* attaches one to happiness, *rajas* to action, and from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance,” and so forth, it follows that when the mind—which consists of the three *guṇas*—is in the state of illumination belonging to the *sattva* portion, happiness arises; and this illumination of the *sattva* portion, occurring through the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*, constitutes sensory happiness.
It produces [pleasure];
for indeed, due to the gradations in the manifestation of the constituent element of existence (*sattvāṃśa*), a gradation in sensual pleasure is observed.
And it must necessarily be admitted that this gradation in pleasure is caused by a gradation in the causes of pleasure.
And if that cause of happiness surpasses all worldly causes of happiness, then the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas* can certainly be accomplished by it.

Therefore, by this principle, when the illumination of the *sattva* portion of the mind occurs by completely suppressing *rajas* and *tamas* through the cause consisting of listening to the meaning of transcendent poetry (*lokottarakāvya*), then the realization of the Self— which is of the nature of indivisible light and caused solely by that [illumination]— is indeed valid as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*).
Therefore they say: "Aesthetic relish (*svāda*) arises from the union with the meaning of the poem; it is the emergence of the bliss of the Self.
This is the manner described [in the verse].

And if that [relish] is a cognition arising from the bliss of the Self, then—having excluded [the Self] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) because [the cognition] proceeds from the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having perceived [the disciple] who was nearby, [the teacher] spoke the truth as to "who he is," beginning with the words: "Out of friendship... and so forth.
If [the disciple's state] were caused by the acquisition of the scriptures, then Brahman would manifest in its unconditioned form;
however, if it were not through the seeing and hearing of this primary poem (kāvyam), [then it would be otherwise].
In that case, what can we do regarding its being variegated by elements such as *rati* (love) combined with the *vibhāvas* and so forth?

This very fact—that the diversity of causes results in this *anubhāva* (the aesthetic experience) established through the perception of sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*)—is such that even when it is variegated by elements like *rati*, its self-luminosity remains opposed to darkness; this will be demonstrated further on.
He states this very point: "Self-luminosity and so forth also [will be explained] according to the method to be described."
Precisely because this taste of Brahman is variegated by elements such as pleasure (*rati*) and so forth, its similarity [to worldly experience] exists;
however, its true nature (*tattva*) has not been stated by the Sūtra.
By the phrase "for the sake of its own nature" (*svarūpārtha*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is excluded from its previously presented meaning.

By this, it is stated that rasa is non-different from self-luminous bliss-consciousness (*svaprakāśānandacid*). *Camatkāra* consists of the expansion of the heart and is synonymous with wonder (*vismaya*). Its status as the vital essence [of rasa] has been stated by the venerable Nārāyaṇa-pāda, the foremost among poets and scholars and the most eminent member of the assembly of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) of our great-great-grandfather.
Regarding this, Dharmadatta states in his own work,
*Vijñapriyā*:
"In that context, he explains *sattva* [as being superior] to *rajas* and *tamas*."

The manifestation of the spectator’s turning away from external objects of cognition is "awakening" (udbodha), which means the production of the effect through the attainment of auxiliary factors (sahakārin).
He demonstrates the attainment of these auxiliary factors with the words "and there the cause.
He establishes their unity with the words "the determinants and so forth" (vibhāvādi).

It is that whose nature (svarūpa) consists of a sense of wonder (camatkāra) accompanied by the bliss that is self-luminous and has as its object both the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, as well as the emotions (rati) and so forth.
And this "wonder" will be described as "astonishment.
We shall explain the cause for the simultaneous existence of such bliss and wonder with the words beginning: "There is an operation of the excitants and so forth."

This is because it will be explained later that the operation called "tasting" (*svādana*)—beginning with the aesthetic manifestation (*vibhāva*)—is the cause of wonder and the cause for the spectators' superimposition of non-difference from the hero, such as Rāma.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*): "consciousness" (*cit*) is self-luminous bliss (*ānanda*), which is knowledge (*jñāna*); the meaning is that its very nature is that [bliss].
This is because the non-difference of knowledge and bliss is accepted.

He explains the term "supramundane wonder" (*lokottaracamatkāra*) as follows: "Wonder" (*camatkāra*) is an expansion of the mind, a distinct cognition produced by a particular conjunction with the self.
He demonstrates that very point with the word "astonishment" (*vismaya*).
And its being the "vital breath" (prāṇa) consists in its existing in a state of coexistence with that [rasa].
The passage beginning with "He said," and so forth, is the speech of Nārāyaṇa himself.
In rasa, the essence—which is aesthetic wonder—is experienced everywhere.
If the essence of aesthetic wonder resides in all [rasas], then the wondrous rasa (adbhuta) exists everywhere;
therefore, the learned Nārāyaṇa declared that the wondrous alone is the rasa.
Thus [it is said].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ña) Regarding "the essence in the flavor" (*rase sāra*), it is the essence because it is the cause for the tasting of the flavor.
The locative case in the phrase "taccamatkārasāratve" (in the state of having that aesthetic wonder as its essence) is used in the sense of a condition (*saptamī* of *satī*).

Since aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) consists of amazement (*vismaya*), it produces an excellence within self-luminous bliss; thus, its "essence" (*sāratva*) consists in its being the generator of a flavor (*rasa*) characterized by a distinct type of bliss.
When this [wonder] is present, the marvelous flavor (*adbhuta-rasa*) can occur even in poetic works whose primary flavors are the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.

And thus, when a rasa such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) has arisen in a general sense, wonder (*adbhuta*) is produced, whereby a preeminent rasa such as the erotic—consisting of a unique aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*)—is generated; this is the meaning.

However, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, the aesthetic relish itself is the wonder, and not a separate astonishment (*vismaya*). Therefore, the inclusion of the wonderful (*adbhuta*) does not apply in all cases.

"Therefore, it is indeed the marvelous (adbhuta)"—the meaning is that, because it generates an excellence of love (śṛṅgāra) and other such sentiments within poetry, [the author] spoke of the marvelous as a rasa as well.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ai) It has also been stated by Nārāyaṇadāsa: "The marvelous alone is the foundation of all rasas."
And because that [rasa] is variegated by components such as *rati* (love) and so forth, it receives the designations of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and the like according to the case;
from the presence of those [components], it receives the designation of *adbhuta* (the marvelous).
"By some" refers to those possessed of prior merit.
As it has been said:
"The meritorious perceive the continuous flow of aesthetic flavor (rasa) like those established in yoga."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭa) Regarding the phrase "by those possessing merit"—in some readings, it appears as "by those abounding in merit. The meaning is that merit alone is the cause both for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and for the activity called "savoring" (*āsvādana*).
For it will be stated later: "That relish does not arise without the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) such as passion.
"This activity called 'relishing' is indeed distinct from the categories of volitional action (*kṛti*) and cognition (*jñapti*)."
And because it will be stated thus:
"Locanā:
(lo, o) those who possess merit."
In the phrase "they cognize," there is likewise a metaphorical usage as before,
because it is impossible for this [consciousness], whose nature is self-luminous, to be an object of cognition,
just as in the case of a yogin.

The meaning is that just as yogis directly perceive pure Brahman as being of the nature of self-luminous bliss-consciousness (*svaprakāśānandacidrūpa*), so too do those possessed of merit [perceive it], even though it is variegated by partial elements such as *rati* (erotic love) and the like.

Thus it has been said: "Aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is of the nature of the wonder of self-luminous bliss, variegated by partial elements such as *rati* which are intensified and integrated with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.

However, some maintain that immediately after the direct perception of bliss integrated with *rati* and the like, there occurs the manifestation of the reality of Brahman—which consists of consciousness and bliss and in which the entire phenomenal world has subsided—just as in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) or in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
As they say: "Then,
when the rasa has been fully completed through the recitation and the so-called *dhruvā* songs,
the spectator, with his mind one-pointedly absorbed in the weight of that aesthetic relish, rejoices inwardly for a moment."
Then, for this [consciousness] which is devoid of objects, its own innate nature remains established,
which manifests as a flow of bliss by which yogins are satisfied.

However, the teachers maintain that nothing more than this is required, because one experiences pleasure precisely through the experience of the variegated [state], and because the subsequent reflective awareness— "I am experiencing pleasure"— is sufficiently accounted for by that alone.

The term *rasa* refers to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that is being continuously extended as a stream. By its being described as "continuously extending," it is indicated that this [flavor], which is a sibling to the tasting of Brahman, possesses a flow that proceeds without interruption.

Although, according to the direction stated in the verse, "Tasting arises from the fusion with the meaning of the poem; it is the emergence of self-bliss," it has been asserted that the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not distinct from the act of tasting itself.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭha) "Due to the fusion with the meaning of the poem" means due to the fusion with that which is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) of the poem, consisting of love and so forth; the sense is: through the repeated cultivation of that.
In reality, however, because the word "saṃbhedāt" contains the suffix *lyap*, it functions as an ablative; thus, [the rasa] is "intermingled with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
Regarding "ātmānanda": the meaning is that its manifestation takes the form of the bliss (*ānanda*) which resides within the self (*ātman*).
And so, the meaning is that for rasa, whose essence is bliss, there is no state other than being tasted (*svādāna*).
Locanā:
(lo, au) "The meaning of the poem" refers to the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
"Due to its commingling" (*tatsambhedāt*)—this is the ablative case used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*; thus, the meaning is "commingled with the excitants and so forth."
Nevertheless, the expression "the flavor is tasted" (*rasaḥ svādyate*) is a usage in the sense of the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*), having accepted an imaginary distinction (*kālpanika-bheda*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Imaginary" means a distinction [posited] by superimposing distinction upon non-distinction.

Regarding the phrase "or in the sense of the object-agent" (*karmakartari vā*): just as in the expression “the husking-vessel splits itself” (*bhidyate kuśūlaḥ svayameva*), where there is a superimposition of difference based on the intention to express both the state of being the object and the state of being the agent for a single husking-vessel, so too here, although there is no difference between the tasted and the tasting, the usage is in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartari*) due to the intention to express a distinction.
Furthermore, it is not the case that in the tasted object there is only the state of being the object (*viṣayatā*) of the tasting.
How, then, can agency be attributed to it?
It must be said that agency is superimposed upon it because of its self-luminosity.
As it has been stated: "For rasa is indeed not different from the very essence of manifestation, since its sole core consists in the state of being relished."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) "Because its sole essence consists in being relished"—here, the word *sāra* (essence) has the sense of *svarūpa* (intrinsic nature).
Thus, it is shown that being relished (*rasyamānatā*) is the object of aesthetic savoring (*āsvāda*).
By virtue of having light as its body, its status as the agent of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) is demonstrated;
thus, its status as both object and agent is established.
The meaning is that because self-luminous consciousness possesses the dual nature of both the illuminated and the illuminator, it is indeed non-different from those two.
Locanā:
[The term] "locana" is either conceptual (*kālpanika*) or figurative (*aupacārika*),
or it is used in the sense of the agent being the object (*karmakartṛ*).

"It is tasted" (*svādyate*) means "it is relished" (*āsvādyate*), in the sense that it is delineated through identification with the *rasa*—such as love (*rati*) and so forth—which has been presented by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this way, one should understand the use of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) in other similar instances as well.
[Objection: But by this much, has it not been stated that *rasa* is unknowable?
Vijñapriyā:
"In the same way elsewhere" means in such passages as "that is perceived" and so forth.
"By this much" means by the statement that rasa is non-different from its aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*).
The meaning of "incognizability" (ajñeyatva) is that it is not graspable by a cognition distinct from itself;
the point is that its status as an object of knowledge (jñeyatva) is unestablished because it cannot be grasped by itself, just like a jar or other objects.
Furthermore, since manifestation (vyañjanā) is a specific kind of cognition, the two [the object and its manifestation] have resulted in being identical.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ta) Anticipating the objection that "since it is indeed apprehended by a cognition dependent on suggestion (*vyañjanā*) which is produced by the *vibhāva* and other factors, it does possess the quality of being graspable by a cognition distinct from itself," he says: "And because suggestion is a specific kind of cognition."
Because the flavor (*vyañjanā*) is a specific kind of cognition dependent upon the flavor, and because it is a specific kind of cognition consisting of the experience of taste;
thus, at that moment, since it would be graspable by a cognition distinct from itself, it follows that it is not an object of knowledge (*ajñeya*).
Consequently, it results in the identity of the flavor-experience and the cognition dependent upon the flavor; hence he says: "the identity of the two."
The meaning is: "of two [cognitions] whose knowledge is dependent on a condiment (vyañjana) whose flavor is inseparable from its relish.

Now, what undesirable consequence follows from this? To answer this, it must first be shown that the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth cannot function as manifestors (vyañjaka), because if they cannot be manifestors, then the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) itself cannot be a manifested object (vyaṅgya); this is the undesirable consequence. This is demonstrated by contrasting the excitants with a lamp, which manifests a jar.
He establishes this with the words "and therefore" (*tataśca*).

Just as a lamp is the manifestor of a jar and the like, the aesthetic factors (*vibhāva*) and so forth lack that same status [of being manifestors]; thus, the collective meaning is that there is a distinction, a separate existence, and a difference between the aesthetic factors and the lamp which manifests the jar.
However, this meaning does not hold according to the literal sense of the words as they are heard.

Because it would follow that the lamp— the cause of the cognition of a jar— would be the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of the jar either by means of its own cognition of its object or by means of the cognition produced by itself, the example "just as a lamp" would be untenable;
therefore, [the text specifies] "by means of this [specific] cognition."
In the third alternative, [the object is established] as in the statement: "For the distinction among cognitions occurs solely through the object, since they themselves are formless.
And thus, that very thing which is the cause of another cognition—distinct from the cognition produced by itself—is established.

The meaning is that even without [prior] knowledge, when an object is already established, a lamp is considered a *vyañjaka* (manifestor). However, the *vibhāva* and other factors are not manifestors like a lamp; rather, they are the very generators (*janaka*) of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, which consist of the experience (*āsvāda*) distinct from the cognition dependent upon the manifestation produced by themselves.
"Otherwise" (*anyathābhāve*) means "in a different state," that is, if they were to act as their own manifestors even with respect to what they themselves produce.
The meaning is: what is the distinction between these [factors] such as the *vibhāva* (determinant) and so forth, and the *kāraka* (grammatical cause)?

The meaning is that there is indeed a difference (*pārthakya*)—that is, a distinct characteristic (*vailakṣaṇya*)—between these two, namely *rasa* and the *vibhāva* etc., on the one hand, and the two, namely the *vyaṅgya* (the manifested) and the *vyañjaka* (the manifestor), on the other, like the case of a jar and its cognition.
It does not mean, however, that there is a mutual difference or distinction between the *vyaṅgya* and the *vyañjaka* themselves.
In that case, on the contrary, since the suggestiveness of rasa itself would be established, such a doubt would be untenable.
*Locanā*:
Regarding the phrase "by this much," the word "by means of the literary work" (*prabandhena*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that there is one [commonality] for the *rasa* when it is defined as being suggested (*vyaṅgya*), because there is no difference in its nature as cognition.
And therefore:
"That which, through its own cognition, is the cause of another's understanding regarding an established object is considered a suggester (*vyañjaka*)."
Just as with a lamp, if there were no change [in its state], what distinction would there be between it and its maker?
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) Having dispelled the suspected identity between the suggester (*vyañjana*) and the relish (*āsvāda*), and establishing the thesis that that which exists in the state of *rasa* lacks the status of being a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyatva*), she says: “If it be true... — Locanā.
(i) The cause of another cognition is the cause of the cognition that manifests [the object].
The meaning is that sound is considered a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) when [its existence] is already established, but not when it is yet to be proven;
for example, as in the case of a lamp.
Indeed, a lamp does not produce a jar or the like;
rather, by its own illumination, it makes manifest that which is already established.
Otherwise, if it were otherwise, it would be a case of establishing what is unestablished.
If it is asked, "In the manner stated above, since the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) are distinct— just like a jar and a lamp— how can rasa be something manifested?",
you have spoken the truth.
*Locanā*:

(Lo, ī) The meaning is that, according to the direction stated—that is, by the path taught by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* and others—the distinctness of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*) implies that the distinctness of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) and the suggested object is established by logic itself.
Indeed, a jar is not identical with the light of a lamp;
for this very reason, they say:
“This activity called ‘tasting’ is indeed distinct from the categories of ‘action’ (*kṛti*) and ‘manifestation’ (*jñapti*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase “from the categories of action and manifestation”: ‘action’ is a productive operation, such as the rotation of a stick and so forth.
*Jñapti* is the operation that makes known (*jñāpaka-vyāpāra*), namely:
denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and suggestion (*vyañjanā*);
the meaning is that [the word] is distinct from those operations.
The term "tasting" (svādanā) means a specific mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose nature is relishing and which generates self-luminous knowledge;
thus, *rasa* is precisely that [modification] as its object.

However, the knowledge dependent on suggestion (*vyañjanā*), which has love (*rati*) and so forth as its objects, is entirely distinct from that. Therefore, it is stated that there is no identity between *rasa* and the knowledge dependent on the suggestion thereof.
And that [rasa], which consists of the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth, is essentially non-different from manifestation (vyañjanā); this is the meaning.

Thus, the logical connection is as follows: through manifestation (vyañjanā), there is simply the cognition of love (rati) and so forth, whereas through the operation called "tasting" (svādana), there is the savoring of rasa.
To the question, "In that case, how is it said that rasa is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya)? he says: "Abhidhādi... [and so forth].

The function called *vyañjanā* (suggestion) is distinct [from denotation and the rest]; the meaning is that rasa is "suggested" in a mediated sense (*paramparayā*), because the passion (*rati*) and so forth of the audience—which serve as the substratum for the superimposition of the suggested lover (*nāyaka*) and so forth—undergoes a transformation into the very form of rasa.
This is the view of the *Locanā*.

"From this very reason" (*ata eva*)—this connects with the distant word "iti" in the phrase "it has been stated that the nature of what is called 'they say' (*āhuḥ*) is suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*). The meaning is: "from this very reason," because rasa is indeed of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).
The phrase "the ancient teachers who know logic say" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
*Kṛti* means action (*karaṇa*);
*jñapti* means knowledge (*jñāna*).
Tasting (*svāda*) is the act of tasting; it is of the kind described in the statement: "Tasting arises from the fusion with the meaning of the poem, resulting in the emergence of self-bliss.
It is "some" (*kaścit*), meaning extraordinary or supramundane (*alaukika*). It is an "activity" (*vyāpāra*), which is non-different from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that constitutes its object.
"It is distinct from the manifestor"—this is the ellipsis.
For this very reason, designations such as "tasting," "savoring," and "experiencing aesthetic wonder" are indeed distinct.
Thus, by us—who are intent on establishing merely that there is an operation distinct from denotation (*abhidhā*) and the rest—it follows that rasa and the like are *vyaṅgya* (suggestible).
Locanā:
(ū) It has been stated that [the word] possesses suggestiveness; the meaning is that this is due to the metaphorical designation of "manifestation" alone.

[Objection: "In that case, since sentiments such as compassion (*karuṇa*) are of the nature of suffering, they would not possess the quality of being a *rasa* (or rather, the state of being directed toward that [bliss] would not exist). To this it is said—*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, dha) "It would not be *rasa* (aesthetic flavor)"—the meaning is that this is because *rasa* consists of self-luminous bliss.
Regarding the supreme bliss that arises even in *rasas* such as the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the experience of sensitive persons (*sacetasaḥ*) is the sole authority (*pramāṇa*) therein. (VisSd 3.4)
Vijñapriyā:

Regarding the phrase "in the aesthetic flavor" (*rase*)— it means that when an aesthetic flavor such as compassion (*karuṇā*) is to be apprehended, the very nature of that compassionate flavor itself arises as bliss,
because there is no bliss apart from the aesthetic flavors.
"An experience of those possessed of sensitivity" means that while sorrow and pain arise from [the aesthetic flavors] such as the erotic only for those who know them [in their ordinary sense],
for the spectators (*sāmājika*), only pleasure arises; in this matter, the experience of those possessed of sensitivity is the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*).
Locanā:
(ṛ) "Is it not so? means:
in that case, the meaning is that *rasa* is of the nature of such bliss.

The expression "pleasure in the rasa" is a metaphorical designation; it refers to those who possess consciousness and aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya) regarding those [rasas] such as compassion and the rest.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), and so forth are included.
Nevertheless, another alternative is stated in order to seal the mouths of those who lack aesthetic sensitivity (*asahṛdaya*):
*Vijñapriyā*: [The text continues...]
The meaning is: even for those whose hearts are not compassionate, suffering arises simply from the knowledge of another's suffering; that is, even for those whose hearts are of such a nature.
Furthermore, when there is suffering among them, no one would be intent upon that [suffering];
for no sentient being with consciousness engages in action for the sake of their own suffering.
Furthermore, since it is observed that everyone engages in compassion and the like with full commitment, they consist of nothing but happiness.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Moreover, in those [states]"—the meaning is that this is another logical inconsistency regarding their being causes of suffering.
Locanā: (lo,
ṝ) She is characterized by dogmatic adherence, but not one who acts under the influence of kings and the like.
He states another logical impossibility: "In the same way, the Rāmāyaṇa and other such works would become causes of suffering. (VisSd 3.5)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ba) "Likewise, [regarding] the Rāmāyaṇa"—here, the Rāmāyaṇa refers to a specific portion of it characterized by the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*). "The consequence of being a cause of suffering"—and thus, no one would engage in listening to it.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) [If it were argued that] the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the great epic of Vālmīki,

[is a source of suffering], then it would follow that literary compositions such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which are dominated by the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇarasa*), must also be causes of suffering, since pathos itself is a cause of suffering.
Now, one might ask: "How can happiness arise from the causes of suffering? To this he says:
*Vijñapriyā*:
"(vi, bha) 'From the causes of suffering'—the grief of others and so forth are indeed the causes of one's own suffering."
The meaning of "how" [is asked] with respect to them:
how can they possess the nature of causes for grief, joy, and so forth, since they depend upon the world? Let it be granted that worldly grief, joy, and the like arise in the world. (VisSd 3.6)
Vijñapriyā:

(Ma) "The state of being a cause" [is established] by relying on worldly convention—because it is observed in the world that sorrow, joy, and so forth arise from causes such as another's sorrow and joy, which are understood to be the causes of one's own sorrow, joy, and so forth; let this be accepted according to the maxim: "Let the wicked man be satisfied."

Having said this, he states: "It is called *alaukika* (transcendental). What harm is there in saying that from all those [objects] which have attained the status of transcendental excitants (*vibhāva*) by virtue of being based on poetry, pleasure is produced? (VisSd 3.7)
Locanā: (lo,
e) "The state of being a cause"— that is, the state of being a cause [is established] because [events such as] Rāma’s exile to the forest have become causes due to their reliance on the world,
and not due to their reliance on poetry.
In the world, but not in poetry;
[these are] worldly, not unworldly.
From these— namely, Rāma’s exile to the forest and so forth.

Indeed, those very things such as Rāma’s forest exile which are called "forests of suffering" (*duḥkhāraṇāni*) in the world, when presented in poetry and drama, abandon the designation of being "causes" (*kāraṇa*) due to their possession of an extraordinary function of manifestation (*alaukika-vibhāvana-vyāpāra*), and instead come to possess the designation of "extraordinary excitants" (*alaukika-vibhāva*).
And from those [objects], such as teeth and minerals, only pleasure arises during sexual union;
Locanā:
because they possess the activity of extraordinary manifestation (*alaukika-vibhāvanā*).
It is not merely by way of being another synonym;
the essential nature of *vibhāvanā* and so forth will be explained [later] as "from the biting of teeth and so on during sexual union."

By means of this specific distinction of place, time, and so forth, that which consists of pleasure may become characterized by suffering, and that which consists of suffering may become characterized by pleasure.
For this very reason, the Sāṅkhyas say: "The phenomenal world (prapañca) has the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion."
And therefore, the restriction that "worldly sorrow, joy, and so forth arise from worldly causes such as sorrow and joy" applies only to the world;
however, in poetry, [it is otherwise], as Locanā says:
(o) Regarding the extraordinary meaning (*alaukikārtha*) in poetry:
since there is the rule that "from all the factors such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, only pleasure (*sukha*) arises," no fault whatsoever [is incurred].
How then is it explained that from the seeing and hearing of the life-stories of Hariścandra and others, even in poetry and drama, tears and the like arise? It is said: [as follows]—
The shedding of tears and so forth are likewise considered [to arise] from the swiftness of the mind.
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "from the swiftness of the mind"—the swiftness of the mind is precisely its state of being compassionate (*sadayatva*).
The sense is that even though there is pleasure, tears fall due to compassion for that [suffering being].
Locanā:
(lo, au) Because of its rapidity—that is, because of its state of melting—there is the arousal of rasa.
If that is so, why is it that such a manifestation of rasa does not arise for everyone from poetry? To this he says:
"That savoring [of rasa] does not arise without the latent impressions (vāsanā) of passion (rati) and the like. (VisSd 3.8)
Vijñapriyā:

"(ra) Without the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and so forth"—thus it has been stated that even the latent impressions of pleasure and so forth produced by merit are a cause for the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
And these latent impressions—both present and past—are the cause of the relish of aesthetic flavor.
In that regard, if the first [condition] were not present, then even those such as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) or elderly Mīmāṃsakas would possess it.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"If the first" means the contemporary one.

Regarding the term *otriyāḥ*: for the Mīmāṃsakas who have grown old [in their studies] do not possess the relish of poetic sentiment (*kāvyarasa*) due solely to their cultivation of logic concerning causal relations and the like; rather, the meaning is that they possess such [sentimental] impressions (*vāsanā*) at that time because of that cultivation.
Nor should it be argued: "Let it simply be said that they lack the relish of poetic sentiment precisely because of the absence of prior impressions (*prāktana-vāsanā*);
why then is the admission of present impressions (*idānīntana-vāsanā*) necessary? This is because [the present impressions are required to account for the specific state of mind at that moment].

Because even for those very same people, by abandoning the practice of logic (*tarka*) and instead practicing the study of poetry (*kāvyānuśīlana*), there is now necessarily the awakening of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which must certainly be stated; for if the second [cause] did not exist, then the awakening of *rasa* that is observed even in some who are practitioners of logic would not occur.
— *Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding the phrase "even for those possessed of passion" (*rāgiṇām api*): this means even for those who possess the experience and cognition of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of poetry. It should not be argued that for them there is no arousal of *rasa* simply because they lack present-day latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
for since the passion for that [poetry] exists—which is the generator of present-day latent impressions—the existence of those impressions is necessarily present.
In reality, however, it is more appropriate to regard the cause as being precisely by way of the nature of a latent impression (*vāsanātvena*).
However, there is no introduction of factors such as "presentness" (*idānīntanatva*) therein; rather, for the ancient Mīmāṃsakas, the very obstacle is their extreme attachment to logic (*tarka*).
And it has been said by Dharmadatta:
"The tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) occurs for those members of the assembly who possess the latent impressions (*savāsanā*)."
But those devoid of latent impressions are like wood, walls, or stones within a theater.

Thus [it is asked]: "But how can it be said that the arousal of the *rasa* such as love (*rati*) in the audience occurs through Sītā and others, who are the causes for arousing the love of Rāma and others?"— [to which the author replies] in the *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, śa) "How so?"—the meaning is: from Sītā and others who have been seen or heard of in dramatic poetry (*nāṭyakāvya*).
Locanā:
(lo, a) "Indeed" (*nanu*) [is used here].

In that view, the arousal of love and other emotions in the audience by means of Sītā and others—who are the causes for arousing love and so forth in Rāma and others—attains the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
There exists a function of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the rest, known as "universalization" (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*);
by its power, [the emotions] such as leaping across the ocean [of Rāma] come into being.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) There is an activity;
it is a common creative act consisting in the superimposition of non-difference from Rāma and others upon the spectator.

The meaning of the verse is that this [capacity] is common to both the superimposition of "belongingness" onto Rāma and Sītā and so forth, and the superimposition of the non-difference of Rāma’s passion and so forth onto one's own passion and so forth.
The suffix *ktin* is used even for the agent (*kartṛ*) precisely because of such usage.
"By its power" means that the cognizer identifies himself with Hanuman and others who possessed such feats as leaping across the ocean; this is the meaning.
He states the reason for this: "by its power."
The meaning is: "by the power of making [them] common.
Since the apprehension of non-difference is possible when there is no apprehension of difference, he says: "by its non-differentiation.
Even in the absence of the apprehension of difference—the meaning is: "by the power of making [them] common."
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) "Commonalization" (*sādhāraṇīkṛti*) means the act of making common (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*). "By its power" means by the power of the operation of commonalization.
The connection is that one realizes one's own self as non-different from that [object].
"Of whom it is near" means:
He explains this with the words "by non-difference from that" (*tadabhedeneti*).
The meaning is as follows:

when the members of the assembly perceive the non-difference [of the actors] from Rāma and others, then through the sight of Rāvaṇa and so forth in drama and the hearing of them in poetry, anger is aroused; consequently, rising from their seats, they proceed to actions such as drawing their bows.
If, however, there were cognition through differentiation (*bhedena*), there would be no arousal of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as anger which is rooted in the self;
and thus, the fault that will be demonstrated immediately hereafter would follow.

As it has been said: "It is cognized without differentiation"—just as, for the proponents of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*), there is a grasping of difference in the cognition of silver regarding mother-of-pearl.
The cognizer realizes his own self as non-different from that [object].
Now, it may be asked: "How can an awakening of enthusiasm for such things as leaping across the ocean arise in a mere human being?
To this, it is said: *Vijñapriyā*: [The answer follows].

(vi, sa) Having thus stated the superimposition of non-difference between himself and Hanuman and others, he raises an objection in order to demonstrate that the arousal of his own enthusiasm occurs precisely through the knowledge of their enthusiasm:
"The arousal of enthusiasm and so forth arises from the conceit of commonality. (VisSd 3.10)
Vijñapriyā:
(h) But how is this so?—because of the conceit of commonality—that is, because of the conceit of non-difference from Hanumān and others within oneself.
Even for ordinary men, there is no fault in [the power of] leaping across the ocean and so forth.
Locanā:

By the power of the conceit of universality—namely, by the force of the conceit of universality that arises within oneself through the influence of the operation of universalization of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth in the manner described;
"of men"—that is, of the members of the audience (*sabhyas*).
He states that even *rati* and the others are perceived through commonality alone—
Vijñapriyā:
"Through commonality" means through the commonality of both.
The meaning is that it is not solely by virtue of being located within oneself, nor solely by virtue of being located within Rāma and others;
rather, even the erotic sentiment (*rati*) and so forth are perceived in that same way through their commonality.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) [refers to] Rati and the others;
it is the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the refined audience.
It is perceived as common [to all];
the meaning is that this occurs precisely through the power of the operation of universalizing the *vibhāvas* and so forth.
If even *rati* and the like were perceived as residing within one's own self, the audience would experience shame, terror, and other such emotions.
Vijñapriyā:
(kha) "From passion and so forth"—that is, by being inherent in oneself; that is, by being inherent in the self alone. Thus, in what follows as well, the term "mere" (*mātra*) is implied.
For if they were inherent in another, there would follow the consequence of their being undesirable.
Locanā:

Regarding the phrase "perceived as being within oneself" (*ātmagatatvena pratītau*), the remainder of the sense is "by way of having Sītā and so forth, who possess the form of the deity and so on, as the cause.
"Unpalatability" (*arasyatā*) means the state of not being relishable.
He states that even the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are first perceived in a general manner:
"Neither 'another's' nor 'not another's,' neither 'mine' nor 'not mine'—in the savoring of that, no distinction of the excitants and so forth exists. (VisSd 3.12)
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the phrase "not of another, not of another"—here too, the meaning is "of another alone," and so forth.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ū) "In the relishing of that" means in the relishing of that rasa.
And thus, the meaning is that the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth themselves cause [the rasa] to be perceived through universalization.
Now, even so, how is it said that these excitants and so forth possess such a non-worldly (alaukika) nature? It is said:
For those who have attained the extraordinary activity of meditative cultivation and so forth,
this extraordinariness is an ornament, not a defect.
From the word "etc. (ādi), [the following are included]: the consequents (anubhāva) and the transitory states (sañcāriṇa).
Among these, the manifestation (vibhāvana) of love and so forth is [defined] by Locanā:
(Lo, ṛ) The meaning is that of the world beginning with passion (*rati*), which is submerged within another latent impression (*vāsanā*) contained within [the mind].
It refers to the induction of a state of fitness for the sprouting of the relish of distinctions.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) Regarding the term "sprout of relish" (*āsvādāṅkura*): its fitness consists precisely in the suggestion (*vyañjanā*) of [emotions] such as love (*rati*).

Since this etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) exists even in the case of the *anubhāvas* and so forth, it is not employed there because the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*). The same should be understood for the subsequent technical definitions of the *anubhāvas* and the *vyabhicāribhāvas*.
*Anubhāvana* is the very act of bringing forth (*bhāvana*) love and so forth, which have been combined, immediately after [their perception] in the form of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṅa):
He says "immediacy" for the sake of clarification.

The meaning is this: for that [emotional state] which has become such—that is, which has reached the stage of the sprout of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*)—there is an entry into the form of rasa by means of the operation called "self-contained tasting" (*svaniṣṭha-svādana*) directed toward joy (*rati*) and so forth.
It should be understood that this is brought about precisely by the determinants (*vibhāva*) and the other factors.
Likewise, "circulation" (*sañcāraṇa*) refers to the thorough movement of that very same state as it has thus come to be.

If the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth function respectively as the cause, the effect, and the auxiliary, how can it be said that all three are causes for the arousal of rasa? To this it is replied:
"For even those [factors] which, according to worldly convention, take the form of cause, effect, or transitory emotion (*sañcārī*)," says Locanā.
In common worldly usage, when there is an awakening of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), those factors such as the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are considered merely causes. (VisSd 3.14)

[Objection: "In that case, how can it be said that there is a single manifestation of them in the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)?"—*Vijñapriyā*: [The meaning of the question] "How [can there be a single manifestation] of all three? is that [the three] lack the status of being causes of the effect [of the aesthetic flavor].
The meaning is that there is a single manifestation in the tasting of the rasa.

That which is being perceived is first called the cause individually; thereafter, all the *vibhāvas* and so forth, combined together, [constitute the cause] for those possessed of sensitivity. (VisSd 3.15)
Through the analogy of the flavoring of a beverage, the rasa becomes something to be savored;
just as from the combination of sugar, black pepper, and other ingredients, there arises, as it were, something unprecedented,
O Locanā.
"Like something unprecedented"—that is, as if distinct from it.

Just as some unique aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) arises from the combination of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth in a dramaturgical performance, so too does it arise here [in poetry]; this is the meaning.

Now, if rasa arises only when the determinants, consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) are combined, how can it be said that it occurs even when only one or two of them are present? It is explained as follows:
If the existence [of the aesthetic flavor] were to arise from the transitory moods (vibhāva) and so forth, it would belong either to both or to one of the two.
"In that case, no fault exists when there is an immediate implication of another [meaning].
*Vijñapriyā*:
"When there is an immediate indication of another"—the meaning is: when there is a swift manifestation of another [sense].
And there is also the implication of something else by virtue of the context and so forth;
for example:
“Long are her eyes, her face is like the lovely autumn moon, her arms droop from the slope of her shoulders, her chest is narrow yet firm with high breasts, and her sides appear as if smoothed down.”
Her waist was measured by a span, her hips were broad, and her feet had uplifted toes; her body was fashioned just as the mind of the Creator desired for a dancer.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ja) Regarding the phrase "long-eyed"—this is a description of the beauty of Mālavikā, the daughter of a king, by King Agnimitra. Her body was created [by the Creator] exactly according to the desire and will of the mind of the supreme dancer.
He says that very thing: "long-eyed"—the arms are bent at their own roots, which are the shoulders; "compact" means not too broad;
and "broad" refers to that [chest] where the breasts are dense—meaning closely pressed against each other—and elevated.
"Pramṛṣṭe" means polished or wiped clean. "Pāṇimitaḥ" means capable of being measured by the palm of the hand.
"Jaghanottarabhāgaḥ" refers to the buttocks; when these are excellent, that constitutes a beautiful hip.
"Udgrā" means elevated;
"herein" refers to one who describes the face.
Locanā.
"Long-eyed" (*dīrghākṣam*):
this is intended according to the meter;

the ellipsis is "created by the Ordainer. The dancer (*nartayitā*) teaches the female dancers how to demonstrate [the state] through the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of having long eyes and so forth.
The sense is that in Mālavikā, this [beauty] exists by virtue of her innate loveliness alone.

Here, although only the excitant (vibhāva) consisting of Mālavikā’s form is described for Agnimitra, who desires her, there is an implied suggestion (ākṣepa) of the transitory emotions (sañcāribhāvas) such as eagerness (autsukya) and of the consequent expressions (anubhāvas) such as the dilation of the eyes, precisely because of their propriety (*aucitya*). This same principle should be inferred even when one thing implies another.
Locanā:
Regarding the phrase "the rejection of others" (*anyākṣepa*)—that is, one or two of the other [factors].
He replies to the one who asserts that "rasa resides in the object of imitation" (*anukāryya*):
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) "The object of imitation"—in drama, the object of imitation is Rāma and others, while the imitator is the actor.
Locanā:
The object of imitation is Rāma and others; the imitator is the actor and the reciter.
Because it is limited, worldly, and characterized by interruptions, [it is not the ultimate reality]. (Viṣṇu-sahasranāma-ṭīkā 3.17)
The awakening of the emotion (*rati*) and so forth belonging to the character being portrayed would not constitute *rasa*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ña): "Because of its limitation" means that the love directed toward objects such as Sītā is limited because it resides solely in [the individual] Rāma and others.
"Because it is worldly"—the meaning is that the love and other emotions residing in that [object] are perceived as such only there [in the real world].

However, in poetry and drama, because of the non-difference between those [real-world] loves and so forth and the [aesthetic] love and so forth, the love and other emotions of the audience—which are the objects of superimposition—are indeed *alaukika* (transcendental).
"In another [context]"—the meaning is: in the case of the love and other emotions of Rāma and others.

The meaning is this: the object of superimposition through non-differentiation from that [actor] is precisely the love (*rati*) and so forth of the audience; this is *rasa*, which is the object of the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) produced by the operation called "tasting" (*svādana*) residing in the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.

For the arousal of Rāma’s love and so forth, born from the sight of Sītā and others, is limited, worldly, and subject to interruption due to the witnessing of drama or poetry; therefore, how could it attain the nature of *rasa*?
(ka) Because this [flavour] possesses properties distinct from these three properties of the [ordinary] rasa;
and [the author] refutes its being located in the imitator—
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) "The imitator"—the imitator is indeed the actor.
[He attains] the state of being Rāghava and others merely through training, practice, and so forth. (Viṣṇu-siddhānta 3.18)
A dancer, while demonstrating [the performance], would not himself be a relisher of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) He says "moreover" (*kiṃca*) to show that when he becomes an experiencer of the meaning and emotional states of the poem, then he too would become a member of the audience (*sāmājika*).
Moreover:
"Through the contemplation of the meaning of the poem, this person also becomes a fit recipient for the status of a connoisseur. (VisSd 3.19)

If, however, even the actor, through his contemplation of the meaning of the poetic work, were to manifest his own self as having the very nature of Rāma and others, then he too would be counted as one among the members of the assembly (*sabhyamadhye*).
Locanā:
(Lo, Au) "He is counted as one among the members of the assembly."
The meaning is that, to this extent, rasa resides solely within the connoisseur (*sabhya*).
It is not something to be made known (*jñāpya*), because its very existence is inseparable from its cognition.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ḍa) Although, according to the aforementioned method, rasa possesses direct perceptibility (*sākṣātkriyamāṇatva*), the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), existence as something future or present due to its occasional nature (*kādācitkatvena*),

the status of being an object of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna-viṣayatva*), and the fact that the cognition thereof is of the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkara-rūpatva*); nevertheless, in order to establish its distinctiveness, we shall— out of curiosity— establish its difference even from a jar or similar object that is directly perceived, by proving its lack of direct perceptibility [in the same manner].

Having refuted the claim made by some that [the Self] is an effect of a specific cause, and out of curiosity wishing to state that it is generally not an effect—and likewise that it is "not thus" (i.e., not future), and so forth—he first states that it is the object of direct perception common to jars and other things, saying: "This is not to be made known. The meaning is: "This is not to be known," because [the suffix -ya] ends in the sense of the causative (*ṇijanta*) rather than the passive (*svārthaka*).
Since the properties of being made known (*jñāpyatva*) and being knowable (*jñeyatva*) are co-extensive, one may follow the literal meaning as it stands.
Furthermore, "unknowability" (*ajñeyatva*) here refers to not being the object of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) other than that which is common to jars and so forth;
for since knowability is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property, its absence is impossible.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "In its own existence," because it is invariably concomitant with [the self]. Since it does not exist without direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), rasa exists only at the moment of direct perception.
But at other times, pleasure and so forth [are known] only as such;

whereas a jar and the like are "jars" even in a state where they are not being directly perceived. Therefore, there is a distinction between them, because for the sake of the sensory contact that causes direct perception, prior existence must necessarily be required.
By this much alone, [the author] will later clarify, out of curiosity, that it is indeed unknowable in a general sense.
Locanā:

"This is not something to be made known"—this means that this *rasa*, because of its non-existence in the absence of cognition, exists only in its state of being (*sattā*) or actual presence (*sadbhāva*).
Furthermore, because there is a lack of evidence for its being unperceived by sentient beings:
for while an object such as a jar, though existent, may sometimes be unknown,
this [self] is not like that.
Because it does not exist apart from cognition,
for this [cognition] consists of a collective mental apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the various aspects (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is not an effect—*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍha) He refutes the view of those who claim that rasa is the effect of a specific cause, with the passage beginning "Since this... and ending with "...therefore, it is not an effect."

The meaning is as follows: by the statement, “the rasa would be experienced through the analogy of the taste of a refreshing drink (*prapānaka-rasa*),” it is asserted that *rasa* consists of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, together with the emotions (*rati*) and so forth. And that collective apprehension is produced by the operation known as *svādana* (tasting).
Some, however, hold that at the same time [as the tasting], such a collective apprehension also arises subsequently through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
They say that rasa is indeed the effect of that [cognition]; he refutes this with the words "because this..."—
for this rasa consists of a collective apprehension (samūhālambana) dependent upon the operation called "tasting" (svādāna).

Therefore, it does not produce an effect, nor does it produce a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) as its effect; for the reason is that it cannot be its own effect, and because there exists no other collective cognition—dependent on manifestation—that arises at its own time.
This is the intended meaning, since the impossibility of something being its own effect is self-evident in this case.
Locanā:

Regarding the phrase "of rasa" (*rasasya*)—the sense is that it is not the case that [rasa] has the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and so forth as its cause; consequently, since no other cause is perceived for rasa, it cannot be an effect.
If rasa were an effect, it would necessarily have the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and so forth as its cause.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṇa) He explains the impossibility of [the cognition] being an immediate effect of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) that arises at the same time as itself: "if the taste were the effect," meaning, if it were the effect of a collective apprehension.

The meaning is that [the aesthetic emotion] would have as its cause the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and so forth taken collectively—that is, it would have as its cause the cognition whose object is the totality of the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas*.
However, if each *vibhava* and so forth were individually the cause of the cognition, this would simply result in what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*).

This is because, by the statement, “The suggested [emotion] is first said to have each [factor] as its cause,” the causality of each individual factor is asserted; and since there is no disagreement regarding something being the effect of those [individual causes], [the collective view is unnecessary].
And consequently, at the time of the apprehension of the rasa, the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth would not be apprehended.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ta):
[The author] asks, "What is the fault in such being the cause of the synthesis of the collection? and answers with the words "And consequently" (*tataśca*).

At the time of the cognition of rasa— that is, at the time of the arising of the cognition of rasa, which consists of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth produced by the operation called "tasting" (*svādana*)— the excitants and other factors would not be perceived;
the meaning is that they would become objects of a cognition produced at that very moment.
Because the knowledge of the cause and the knowledge of the effect are never observed to exist simultaneously;
for it is simply impossible for the persistence of the knowledge of the cause to coincide with the arising of the knowledge of the effect.
Because there is simply no possibility of the simultaneous arising of cause and effect, he says: "of the cognition and the cognition of its effect.
Here, the word "cognition" is used precisely with reference to the subject at hand.
This is because there is no simultaneous production of merely the cause and the effect;
nor should it be argued that the previously arisen [cognition] itself is the collective apprehension dependent on the manifestation,
for one experiences a collective apprehension distinct from the collective apprehension consisting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which depends on the operation known as "tasting" (*svādana*).
And because its acceptance would be futile;
for it is not possible for the cognition of the touch of sandalwood and the cognition of the pleasure produced by it to occur at one and the same time.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, da) He demonstrates the impossibility of the simultaneous arising of the cognition of the cause and the effect with the words "For [the fragrance] of sandalwood...

The intended meaning is that since the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is perceived precisely as having the nature of being a unified mental apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, it cannot have the cognition of the excitants and so forth as its cause.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, dha) Therefore, he concludes that rasa consists precisely in being a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), and not in being produced by a collective apprehension— this is expressed by the words "of rasa.
By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "precisely as having the nature of a collective apprehension," the possibility of its being produced by a collective apprehension is excluded.
He says that very thing: "not from the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth.
Here too, "cognition" (jñāna) refers to a collective apprehension (samūhālambana).
Thus, it is only the status of rasa as being produced by a collective apprehension that is refuted, not its status as an effect [of anything at all].
He will state later, on the grounds of the general absence of being an effect (*kāryatva-sāmānyābhāva*), that it is for this very reason [that it is not eternal].
*Locanā*:
"Not eternal"—he states the reason for the absence of eternity.
Regarding the phrase "abandoned by prior cognition," the meaning is "due to the absence of prior cognition.

Now, one might object: if there is an absence of permanence because of the absence of prior cognition, then it would follow that other permanent entities also do not exist. To this, he says: "non-cognition... [and so forth].
Of this essence:
it is not eternal, for it is devoid of prior cognition;
indeed, at the time when there is no cognition, even its existence is not found. (3.21)
Locanā:
(vi, na) The absence of permanence is indeed evident;
he states this by saying "not eternal."
"Prior to perception" means that prior to perception, it is abandoned and non-existent;
he demonstrates this very point by saying "at the time of non-perception."

Indeed, it is not the case that an eternal entity is non-existent at the time of its non-perception, nor is it something yet to come, because its nature is directly one consisting of bliss and self-luminous. Regarding this, he says it is not "yet to come": for how could that which is being directly experienced be something yet to come?
The meaning is this: for whatever entity "future-ness" is an inherent property (*sahaja-dharma*), that entity will indeed always be future.
This is established by the logic just stated, because its nature is not distinct from [the nature of] an effect or a signified object (*kārya-jñāpya-vilakṣaṇa-bhāvāt*).
Furthermore, it is not even present, because its nature is not distinct from an effect or a signified object.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, pa) Nor can it be "about to come into being. Although it is difficult to deny that "being about to come into being" is simply non-existence prior to perception, nevertheless, because another future object lacks the essential nature of being a direct manifestation consisting of bliss, its very difference from that [consciousness] is stated here as the absence of "being about to come into being," out of a desire for poetic curiosity.

Because it is the object of the reflective awareness of discerning people regarding its manifestation and so forth, and because it is clearly experienced by them as consisting of supreme bliss. (VisSd 3.23)
Non-conceptual cognition is not accepted as its apprehender.
Vijñapriyā (vi, pha):
Out of curiosity, he also states the absence of presentness—namely, "to be produced or made known."

Although it was previously shown that there is an absence of being knowable by a cognition common to [all things] such as a jar, and an absence of being the effect of a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*),
nevertheless, having merely superimposed the absence of being an effect and being knowable upon it out of curiosity, this was stated.
Thus, the meaning is that because that which is distinct from an effect or what is knowable is unreal (*alīka*), it does not exist in the present.
Since that which is of the nature of self-luminosity has only itself as its grasper, yet that [grasper] is not indeterminate (nirvikalpaka), he says: "vibhāvādi" and so forth.
That "reflection upon it" (tatparāmarśa) is a cognition having that [set of factors] as its collective object (samūhālambana).
"Because it has that as its object" means because it makes itself its own object by itself.

In some readings, "because it has that as its primary [object]" (*tat-pradhānatvāt*) occurs; in that case, "that" refers back to each respective cognition, and the meaning is "because it has that as its primary [object]," which is to say, because it is produced by that.
In either case, there is simply an absence of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*).
In the first case, because the collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) of the [four] meditative stages (*vibhāva*, etc. is conceptual (*savikalpaka*);
and in the latter case, because it lacks non-conceptuality due to being produced by a [prior] cognition.
Because only the knowledge produced by [prior] knowledge is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), he states another reason: "supreme bliss" (*parānanda*).
By showing this specific mode (*prakāra*), its state of possessing a mode (*saprakāratva*) is demonstrated.
And thus, it is not non-conceptual, because only knowledge devoid of modes (*niṣprakāraka*) is such [non-conceptual].
Locanā:
(lo, ī) Non-conceptual knowledge—there indeed exists first a non-conceptual knowledge consisting of mere observation (*ālocana*).
The phrase "knowledge similar to such-and-such, born from a pure object" refers to the manner previously described;
the application of the term "grasper" (*grāhaka*) toward that [knowledge] is merely figurative (*upacāra*).
The meaning is that this very essence (*rasa*), when being apprehended, does not exist as non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*).

Likewise, for non-conceptual cognition, even its object [is not a conceptual construction]. In that case, regarding the statement "that which is intended to have the status of a grasper," there is no metaphorical usage; nor is there one because of the absence of the capacity for association with verbal expression. (VisDh 3.24)
"Perceivable through conceptual cognition"—*Vijñapriyā*:
Out of curiosity, he also states its lack of perceivability through conceptual cognition, saying "by such verbal expression," etc. (*vi*, *ba*).

Although the fact that [the object] is cognizable by conceptual cognition is established simply by demonstrating the reasoning for the absence of non-conceptuality in its grasper, nevertheless, its non-cognizability [by that grasper] has been stated out of curiosity, by way of its distinction from other things cognizable by conceptual cognition.
He states that very distinction: "Thus, by means of verbal expression," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is because the rasa does not exist as something to be expressed by the words residing in the poem;
rather, its status as an object of knowledge occurs solely through the expression of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, and not by means of the words contained in the poem.
On the contrary, it will be stated that if that [rasa] were expressed by its own word within that poem, the fact of being expressible by its own word would indeed be a defect.
On this very point, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has also said: "But the meaning characterized as rasa and so forth should not be expressed by its own name."

The statement that "this [flavor] is possessed of rasa" and so forth—expressed by the word *tat* (that) situated within that poem—refers to another category of object (*padārthāntara*) cognizable through conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), which must be expressed by the very words situated within that poem; this constitutes its distinction [from other objects].
For it is only those things cognizable through conceptual knowledge that possess the fitness for the application of verbal expression.
But it is not so for rasa.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, bha) The remainder [of the sense] is that the fitness for application belongs to the word situated within that poem.
