And that [sorrow] arises from the determinants (vibhāva) such as the knowledge of reality;
it produces the consequents (anubhāva) such as dejection,
and is perceived through frequent and intense sighing and breathing.

Thus, in the context of describing the essential nature of all these transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), the mention of the determinants (*vibhāvas*) and consequents (*anubhāvas*) is intended for the sake of their own comprehension by great poets within the great epics (*mahākāvyas*), even when they are indicated through those [determinants and consequents] according to the principle of the fault of being directly expressed by their own words (*svaśabdavācyatva*), which will be discussed later.
Furthermore, the intention is that even the recognition of its own nature (*svarūpa*) becomes exceedingly easy in this way:
"Alas! By one desiring to fashion a covering for the hole in a clay pot with sand, [this right-spiraling conch is used]."
"I have reduced it to powder."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) "The phrase 'the earthen jar' is easy to understand.

By this indirect expression, it is understood that by me, a base person performing evil deeds for the sake of warding off slight worldly suffering, the ultimate happiness of the next life has been destroyed."
And here, the self-reproach due to one's own performance of evil deeds is indeed self-contempt.
Locanā:
(Lo, e) "Like an earthen jar," etc.

In this regard, self-reproach is the thought: "Alas, I have destroyed this body which is capable of accomplishing the supreme good by being intent upon the enjoyments of this worthless saṃsāra; shame on me!
Then follows agitation (āvega):

Avega is agitation; therein, that born of rain consists of the contraction of the limbs, while that born of portents consists of trembling of the limbs, and that born of fire consists of being overwhelmed by smoke and the like. (VisSd 3.143)
From the sight of kings fleeing in terror and so forth, there arises the appearance of weapons, serpents, and the like;
from elephants and such, there arises their paralysis, trembling, and so on; and from wind filled with dust and the like, [the same occurs]. (VisSd 3.144)
From the desirable arise joys;
from the undesirable, sorrows; and others should be understood accordingly.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṅa) Regarding *āvega* (agitation): it is a state of bewilderment or confusion caused by the sudden appearance of an unexpected object. He describes its various effects, which arise from diverse causes.
"Born of the rain": the meaning is that when that [rain] has arisen, the limbs become compacted.
Locanā:
In the year born of rain— that is, occurring during the rainy season— there is despondency due to lack of control and stiffness.
There is an encounter with weapons such as arrows and the like,
and an assault from all sides by *nāgas*, meaning elephants.
The meaning is that others, such as those born from this [lineage], are renowned in the world as superior.
Among them, an example of one born of an enemy is as follows: "Disregarding the king who was saying, 'Worthy of honor! Worthy of honor!', that elder brother of Bharata departed."
Then he fixed his gaze, with its pupils wide and fierce, like the blazing flame of the wrath of a Kṣatriya.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) "Arya, worthy one"—this is spoken by Daśaratha out of agitation upon seeing Paraśurāma standing before him as an enemy of Rāma.
Disregarding Daśaratha who was speaking the first line, Rāma, the elder brother of Bharata, fixed his gaze, with its pupils dilated, toward the direction in which [Paraśurāma] was situated.

What kind of gaze? One whose very nature is the flame of the fire of the Kṣatriya’s wrath. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "on account of the flight and so forth," what is included is the state of bringing the *arghya* offering and the like, occurring when agitation has been produced in the sages. — Locanā.
In the first quarter of the verse beginning with "ardhyam," there is agitation (*āvega*).
Other [instances] should be inferred in the same way.
Now, dejection (*dainya*):
Dejection (*dainya*) is a lack of splendor caused by poverty and the like; it produces impurity and so forth. (VisSd 3.145)
Locanā: (lo, au) Dairgya is protractedness; dāridrya is poverty;
anaujasya is the loss of vitality (ojas).
For example:
"This husband of mine is old and blind, lying upon a couch; the house remains only as its pillars."
"The time for the arrival of the rains has come near, yet there is not even news of my child's well-being;
the jar of oil, carefully collected drop by drop, is broken"—seeing her daughter-in-law thus distressed and languid from the weight of her pregnancy, the mother-in-law weeps for a long time.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) “By poverty and so forth,” etc.; from the word “and so forth” [is meant] by the non-attainment of what is desired and by anxiety.
Lack of vigor is weakness.
"Old and blind"—this is a description of the weeping caused by the breaking of a jar of oil belonging to a woman whose husband is old, blind, poor, and away from home, and whose son is also absent;
it refers to the state of being reduced to mere pillars and beams when the upper roof-structure has collapsed.
A drop of oil— not much oil— belonging to his son Vatsa who had gone abroad; and that [oil] was collected for the purpose of his daughter-in-law’s delivery.
Now, fatigue (*śrama*): fatigue is the exhaustion resulting from sexual pleasure, walking, and so forth, which causes labored breathing, sleep, and the like.
For example:
“Sītā, who was as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower, having walked only three or four steps with haste even in the vicinity of the city—
” Locanā: (lo, a) *Tricaturāṇi* means three and four.
Repeatedly saying, "How much further must we go?", Rāma brought about the first descent of her tears.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) "Immediately outside the city"—this is a description of the area just outside the city of Sītā as she set out for her forest dwelling.
"In the environs" means in the immediate vicinity.
Regarding "the first descent":
in the abduction of Sītā, however, there would be increasingly profuse shedding of tears.
Now, as for intoxication (mada):
Intoxication, born from the consumption of liquor, is a mixture of delusion and bliss.
And by this [wind], the best person lies down; the middling one laughs and sings; and even the base-natured one speaks harshly and weeps. (VisSd 3.147)
For example:
"Amidst the three cups of wine, the playful jesting of the fair-browed women proceeded, consisting of the artful composition of crooked speech, accompanied by laughter that revealed hidden secrets."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) Regarding "delusion-bliss" (*sammohānanda*): delusion (*sammoha*) is a cognition different from one's ordinary state of mind.
Conjunction (*sambheda*) means meeting.
"Amunā" means by this intoxication; "uttamādayaḥ" refers to those who drink liquor.
Regarding "prātibham": *trisarakam* is honey-wine (*madhumadirā*); for the fair-browed women who had attained a flood of flashes of wit (*pratibhā*) through that, a jesting conversation began.
The compound is analyzed as "one whose secret history was both hinted at and revealed suddenly."

Here, through the attainment of a multitude of mental images (*pratibhāsa*) by means of enigmatic speech (*vakravākya*), there arises—by virtue of the consumption of honey-wine (*madhu-madya*)—a cognition resembling the intended cognition; and through laughter and jesting, there is bliss (*ānanda*).
Locanā:
The blending (*saṃbheda*) of delusion (*sammoha*) and bliss (*ānanda*) is their mixture (*miśraṇa*).
*Prātibha* is simply *pratibhā* (intuitive flash).
There are three kinds of intoxicants: *gauḍī*, *mādhvī*, and *paiṣṭī*.
Now, as for dullness (*jaḍatā*)—
Lack of comprehension would be dullness [caused] by seeing or hearing what is desired or undesired;
in that state, there occur such things as staring with unblinking eyes and remaining silent.

As it says in my Prakrit poem, *Kuvalayāśvacarita*: “Only that pair of young people remained there for a mere moment near the funeral pyre, their eyes fixed upon one another, slow with tears, as if they were painted in a picture.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ña) Furthermore, "that"— namely, that pair of young lovers, their slow glances moist with tears directed at one another,
stood there for a mere moment nearby as if fixed in a painting.

Thus is the Sanskrit [text]. The meaning is that for a mere moment, that young couple—appearing as a husband who has returned from a long journey and a wife staying at home—stood nearby there, as if merely fixed in a painting.
That young couple appeared like a husband who has returned from a long journey and a wife remaining at home.

The word *navara* is a regional term (*deśī*) meaning "only. Of what sort is he? His gaze is slow and moistened by being fixed upon one another; here, there is a state of dullness (*jaḍatā*) arising from the sight of the desired object.
Locanā: (lo,
i) "Immediately thereafter," that pair of youths, their moist and languid glances cast at one another,
remained for a mere moment as if fixed in a painting, having conveyed their signal.
A youth and a young woman are "yuvānau"; the pair of them [is *yuvatyugalam*]. Here, due to the observation of what is desired, there is dullness (*jaḍatā*).
Thus...
Now, regarding ferocity (*ugratā*): Ferocity is a state of violence arising from offenses such as [the teacher's] valor;
in this regard, there are sweating, shaking the head, threatening, striking, and so forth. (VisSd 3.149)
For example:

"This arm of mine, which grows weary even at being struck by playful blows from lovely *śirīṣa* flowers— blows obtained through the affectionate jesting of a loving friend— shall fall like the sudden staff of Yama upon the head of anyone who raises a weapon against your body to slay you."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) This is Mādhava’s speech directed toward Aghoraghaṇṭa, who is intent on cutting down Mālatī:
"Her body, which grows weary even from being struck by delicate śirīṣa flowers—obtained through the playful laughter of her affectionate friends—[cannot endure this]."
The meaning is: "May this arm of mine fall upon your head—upon you who are raising a weapon for the sake of slaying this body—like a sudden rod of Yama;
'sudden' (akāṇḍa) means unexpected.
Herein lies the heroism of Mādhava and the transgression of Aghoraghaṇṭa.
Fury belongs to Mādhava.
Now, delusion (moha):
delusion is a state of mental confusion caused by fear, the onset of suffering, or obsessive brooding.
It causes fainting, loss of consciousness, falling, dizziness, blindness, and so forth.
As it is said:
"When her senses were paralyzed by a delusion arising from an intense shock, Rati, unaware of her husband's calamity, for a moment felt as if she had been granted a favor."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) "Delusion" (moha) means state of mindlessness; it is the absence of mind regarding an object, which is to say, the loss of cognition.

Regarding the phrase "tīvrābhiṣaṅge" (in the intense affliction): when Kāmadeva was burnt by Hara, Rati, due to delusion and the loss of her knowledge, appeared for a moment as if she had performed a service.
He demonstrates that service with the word "ajñāna" (ignorance).
By what kind of intense delusion and by what kind of affliction—born of misfortune—was he overcome?
Furthermore, by what kind?
By that which arrests and obstructs the functioning of the senses, namely their capacity as perceivers.
Locanā:
(lo, ī) Intensity;
fearlessness; defeat.
Now, awakening: Awakening is the arrival of consciousness resulting from causes that remove sleep;
it produces yawning, stretching of the limbs, closing of the eyes, and looking about with the body. (VisSd 3.151)
For example:

"Young women, having first awakened even though they had fallen asleep last of all after attaining the bliss of sleep from the exhaustion of long lovemaking, do not break the embrace of their lovers' firm circle of arms, remaining with their limbs unmoving."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) "Exhausted by long dalliance," etc. The young women, having lain down after the hero for his final sleep, though awakened even before he was, remained with their limbs unmoving; thus they avoided the breaking of the embrace of their beloveds' firm circle of arms.
The meaning is that they do not act.
Here, "awakening" (vibodha) is indeed the expressed meaning (vācya).
Now, "dream" (svapna)—
Dream is the experience of objects by one who has entered into sleep, which brings about anger, agitation, fear, exhaustion, pleasure, pain, and so forth. (VisSd 3.152)
For example:
"When you were somehow obtained by me through a dream-vision for the sake of a merciless embrace, as I held my arms outstretched toward the sky, surely many teardrops,
as large as pearls, fell upon the young leaves of the trees before the local deities who were watching."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) "O Sky, [speak] to me.
This is the Yakṣa’s report of his own activities to his beloved through the medium of a cloud.

When you appear in their vision, as the local deities (*sthalī-devatā*) behold me with my arms outstretched toward the sky for the sake of a merciless embrace, do not the teardrops—large as pearls—fall repeatedly upon the young shoots of the trees?
Indeed, they do fall; such is the meaning.
Now, regarding epilepsy (apasmāra): Epilepsy is a derangement of the mind arising from possession by spirits and the like;
it causes trembling of the body, perspiration, frothing at the mouth, salivation, and so forth. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.153)
"He apprehended the lord of rivers as if possessed by an epilepsy: embracing the ground, roaring loudly, with great waves in the form of tossing arms, and foaming at the mouth."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṇa) "Āśliṣṭabhūmim"—this Kṛṣṇa suspected the ocean, the lord of rivers (*āpagānām nadīnām pati*), to be afflicted by epilepsy. He states the characteristics of one suffering from epilepsy with the words beginning "āśliṣṭa," and so forth.
One suffering from epilepsy also falls to the ground; here, "apasmāra" refers to epilepsy when it is remembered as occurring in a person being placed upon the ocean. Now, regarding pride (garva):
Pride (*garva*) is intoxication (*mada*), arising from power, wealth, learning, noble birth, and so forth;
it causes contempt, playful gestures, the display of limbs, lack of decorum, and the like. (VisSd 3.154)
In that regard, pride of valor is as follows:
"As long as I am bearing arms, what is the use of other weapons?
Or rather, if something has not been accomplished by my missile, by whom could it be achieved?"
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ta) Pride (*garva*) is the display of oneself with graceful gestures while showing contempt for another.
The passage beginning with "dhṛta" is clear.
Now, regarding death:
death by means of weapons and the like is the abandonment of life through such acts as prostrating one's limbs.
For example:
"Struck in her heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma, the god of love, that night-stalker woman,
sprinkled with fragrant sandalwood-paste of her own blood, departed for the abode of the Lord of Life."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
tha) "By means of arrows and so forth" means that such a death is not an invariable concomitant state.
However, this is merely a mention of death;
even the passage beginning with "Rāma, the god of love," etc., is an illustration of death alone.
But death in the form of a transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) should be described as being virtually already occurred.
That she was not born [of a womb] will be stated later.

Regarding the phrase "Rāma-manmatha": that night-stalker Tāḍakā herself, as a woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*), went to the dwelling of the Lord of Life—Yama—who is the Lord of Life and the husband of her own life, acting as her escort. Of what sort was she? Rāma himself was the God of Love (*manmatha*); he is her slayer, and his arrow alone is the shaft that kindles passion. She was struck in the heart by that very arrow.
Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is sprinkled with *raktacandana*—blood itself rendered fragrant by distinguished perfumes—which [is denoted by] *Locanā*:
(*lo*, *u*) *rāma*.
Jīviteśa is Yama, the lord of life and the master of the vital breaths.
Now, regarding indolence (ālasya):
indolence is a state of stupor caused by fatigue, pregnancy, and so forth, which brings about yawning, smiling, and other such symptoms. (VisSd 3.155)
For example:
"The young woman, languid from the weight of her pregnancy, does not adorn her limbs in that way, nor does she speak to her friend in that way; she yawns repeatedly while sitting."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "Yawning-smile" (*jṛmbhāsmita*) is laughter accompanied by yawning.
"Not so," and so forth, is easy to understand.
Now, indignation (amarṣa): Indignation is a state of intense fixation arising from censure, insult, humiliation, and the like;
it manifests through redness of the eyes, shaking of the head, knitting of the brows, and gestures of defiance. (VisSd 3.156)
As it is said: "I shall perform penance for my transgression against you, who are worthy of worship;
but I will never defile the great vow of wielding the sword."
Now, regarding sleep:
Sleep is the closing of the mind, arising from fatigue, intoxication, and the like;
it is the cause of yawning, the closing of the eyes, labored breathing, the stretching of the limbs, and so forth. (VisSd 3.157)
As it is said:
"Speaking words both meaningful and meaningless with slow syllables, her eyes half-closed in sleep— she exists in my heart as if she were painted there."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
dha) "sārthakā" refers to this statement made by one remembering a certain beloved who was asleep.
Now, regarding *avahitthā* (concealment): *Avahitthā* is the concealment of outward signs such as joy and the like, caused by fear, respect, shame, and so forth;
it consists of engaging in other activities, speaking otherwise than one feels, looking away, and so on. (VisSd 3.158)
For example:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing at her father's side with her face cast downward, began counting the petals of her play-lotus."
Vijñapriyā: (vi, na) Attachment to other activities is engagement in another task;
speaking otherwise and looking otherwise are forms of action different from those arising from joy.
"Speaking thus" means while Maheśa was speaking words concerning the event of Pārvatī’s marriage;
in this context, the counting of the lotus petals is performed in a different manner.
Now, longing (autsukya): Longing is the inability to endure the passage of time due to the non-attainment of what is desired;
it produces mental distress, haste, perspiration, long sighs, and so forth. (VisSd 3.159)
For example:
"He alone is the bridegroom who took away my maidenhood," and so forth (p.

In this regard, that which was stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* concerning the primacy of *rasa* should be understood as already implied by the fact that even a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), by virtue of possessing the quality of being tasted, is denotable by the term *rasa*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
The verse beginning with "yaḥ kaumāraharaḥ" has been explained previously.
Here, in the category of longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), there is likewise eagerness (*autsukya*).

Because it possesses the quality of being a flavor (*rasa*)— meaning that while having the quality of a flavor implies its imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), this is also present in a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*)—
in this view, the semblance of love (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*) is not the primary element here.
Nevertheless, by the phrase "the mind yearns," it is precisely astonishment (*vismaya*) that appears as the primary element in the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).

Since this [astonishment] is both the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhutarasa*) and a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) within a verse depicting a semblance of love (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*), it is appropriate to regard it as a transitory emotion.
Furthermore, because it is suggested here by a self-contained sentence, it possesses primacy relative to the semblance of love.
Nor should it be argued that the marvelous (*adbhuta*) alone is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in this case;

for the marvelous becomes the flavor of wonder only when its object is similar to a composition of qualities that transcend the world, not when it has any other object, even if that object serves as the basis (*ālambana*) for the marvelous.
For it will be stated later: "The basis is considered to be an object that transcends the world."
And it is said: "Furthermore, the greatness of his virtues shall serve as an incitement.
In this context, the very absence of longing is the object of wonder.
"Gatārtham" means that the meaning has been understood.
The meaning is that in that context, the term "rasa" refers specifically to a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Now, as for madness (*unmāda*): "Madness is a delusion of the mind caused by desire, grief, fear, and so forth."
One laughs, weeps, sings, and prattles at inappropriate times. (VisSd 3.160)
As in my own verse:
"O brother bee!
While you were wandering all around, did you see my beloved, who is dearer to me than life?"
(Experiencing a humming sound with joy: "I am amazed! 'Om,' my friend?
Tell me that quickly."
"What does she resolve upon? From where does she come? And of what nature is she?"
Vijñapriyā: (vi, pha) "O brother, O bee!"—
this is an utterance addressed to the bee by one who is maddened by separation.
The passage beginning with "jhaṅkāra" and so forth is a prose commentary (*cūrṇaka*) in the middle [of the verse].
The phrase "Do you say 'Om'? is for the purpose of accepting the very sound *jhaṅkāra*, because it is understood as being of the nature of the word "Om."
"What does this heroine of mine intend to do, and what is her state?"—this is the meaning of "how.
Now, as for doubt (*śaṅkā*):
"Doubt is the conjecturing of an undesirable outcome based on the cruelty of another, one's own faults, and so forth."
It causes discoloration, trembling, loss of voice, looking toward the sides, and parching of the mouth.
As in my own verse:
"At the end of the night, her limbs tormented by nails pressed down by the force of his breath, this slender-limbed woman applies sandalwood paste for a long time;
she repeatedly applies red lac to her lower lip which has been bitten by teeth, casting her eyes about in agitation on all sides."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ba) "By another's cruelty" means that apprehension (*śaṅkā*) is the contemplation of misfortune due to another's harshness, such as one's own faults and so forth.
"By the lord of her life"—this refers to the slender-limbed, emaciated woman.

Casting her eyes apprehensively all around, having become suspicious of her friends, she applies sandalwood paste to those limbs upon which the lord of her life has left nail-marks, and repeatedly applies red lac to her lower lip where he has inflicted bites with his teeth; such is the meaning.
In this case, the very instruction of her friends is the source of joy;
and the fact that the nail-marks and so forth are caused by derisive laughter and the like is the fault of the self. — Locanā.
(lo, ū) "By the Lord of Life" (prāṇeśena):
here, the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Now, the traditional teaching (*smṛti*):

Memory is said to be the cognition whose object is a thing previously experienced, which is brought about by similar cognitions, reflections, and so forth, as well as by such acts as raising the eyebrows. VisSd 3.162.

As it is said by me: "I remember that smiling face of the lotus-eyed one— how it was cast down with bashfulness upon seeing her friend approach, while her eyes were fixed somewhere with feigned intent, and she had already begun a slight, sidelong glance with pupils dilated."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, bha) "Toward me with feignedness" means: when she had cast her eyes somewhere with feignedness—that is, while her eyes were directed elsewhere—my gaze reached the path of her vision, and [she cast] a sidelong glance with pupils dilated (or projected).
I remember that smiling face;

moreover, what kind of smile was it? Seeing her friend approach with a bashful, yet unconcealed, downward glance—having realized that the hero was a rogue because of the heroine’s slightly smiling expression under her armpit, and having understood that very smile of the friend as well.
The downward turning of the heroine's face, however, is due to shame arising from her friend’s perception of her own lack of respect [for him].
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) "May he look at me"—this being so, the sense is that she feigns this, thinking, "It has never been my desire to cast my eyes elsewhere than upon him."
"Avāñcita" means bent down.
Now, as for "mati": *mati* is the determination of meaning through following the path of policy (*nīti*) and so forth.
Smiling, fortitude, contentment, and great respect arise from that.
For example:
"Without doubt, my mind desires her, for she is capable of accepting a husband;
for the inclinations of the inner sense are the authority of the virtuous regarding matters that are subjects of uncertainty."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ma) "Without doubt, she is fit for acceptance by a Kṣatriya"—this is the speech of Duṣyanta, who, having seen Śakuntalā and subsequently attained consolation after [initially] perceiving her as a Brāhmaṇa girl. The meaning is that she is undoubtedly suitable for acceptance by a Kṣatriya, and is certainly not a Brāhmaṇa girl.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because my noble mind... Noble (*ārya*) means excellent due to being free from improper desire; my mind, having formed a longing, is desirous of her.
Here he states a corroborative illustration (*arthāntaranyāsa*): "For among the virtuous..."
Regarding matters that are subjects of doubt, the internal mental processes of the wise indeed serve as the authoritative means for dispelling uncertainty.

Here, because the specific quality of one's own mind—its capacity for definitive discernment—is presented through the general minds of the wise, there is an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).
Now, [concerning] the disease:
Disease, such as fever and the like, is caused by wind and other humors, producing symptoms such as the desire for earth and trembling.
In that regard, when it consists of heat (dāha), there is the desire for earth and so forth;
when it consists of cold (śaitya), there is trembling and so forth.
A clear example:
*Vijñapriyā* comments on "a clear example" as follows: "Like a young bride separated [from her husband], she falls to the ground, afflicted by the heat."
"Like a plantain tree shaken by the wind, my beloved trembles, afflicted by fever. Thus [ends the section on trembling].
Now, regarding fear (trāsa):
"Fear caused by thunderclaps, lightning, meteors, and the like, brings about trembling and other such effects. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.164)
For example:
"With their thighs brushed by darting fish, their gazes wavering with alarm,
and the sprouts of their hands trembling, the celestial damsels became objects of sight even for their own female companions."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ra) Regarding "parisphurat" and so forth—this is a description of the fear of the apsarases who were distressed by fish that had entered their thighs during a water-sport.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "they even became objects of sight for the circle of female friends."
Let there be visibility for another person who does not know that her thighs were touched by a fish; however,
on another day, even for her friends who do know— this is the meaning—
the reason being the intense terror arising from the suspicion of a snake bite or similar danger.
Now, regarding *vrīḍā* (shame): shame is the absence of audacity (*dhārṣṭya*), caused by misconduct, which brings about such things as the lowering of the face.
For example:
“‘Toward me with deceit’—and so forth” (p. 173).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding the phrase “the absence of audacity”—audacity (*dhārṣṭya*) is a lack of shame.

"Mayi sakapaṭam" and so forth is an illustration of *smṛti* (remembrance). Therein, by the phrase "with shame, looking downward," *lajjā* (shame) is indicated. Now, *harṣa* (joy)— [The text continues: ...is illustrated by the verse beginning with "atha harṣaḥ. In that context, the verse starting with "mayi sakapaṭam" serves as an example of *smṛti*. Therein, through the expression "with shame, looking downward," *lajjā* is expressed. Next is *harṣa*: [the text continues].
Joy (harṣa), however, is the clarity of mind resulting from the attainment of a desired object, which causes tears, a faltering voice, and so forth.
For example:
"Having finally beheld his son's face, the father— like a destitute man who has found a jar of treasure—
was so overcome with joy that he could not even sustain his own body, just as the ocean swells at the rising of the moon."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, va) "Having observed"—that is, having looked at the face of Raghu—this is a description of Dilīpa. "Nidhānakumbhasya" means "of the treasure-pot. "Mūrcchitaḥ" means "increased" or "augmented."
Now, regarding envy (*asūyā*): Envy is the intolerance of another's excellence due to arrogance;
it manifests through the proclamation of faults, the knitting of eyebrows, contempt, anger, and gestures. (VisSd 3.166)

For example: "Then the Lord of Cedi could not endure the honor bestowed there in the assembly upon the enemy of Madhu by the son of Pāṇḍu; for the minds of the proud are envious of the prosperity of others."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, śa) "Asūyānyeti"—the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is intolerance (*asahiṣṇutā*) toward the excellence of another's qualities, such as their haughtiness, egoism, and supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Now, "there" (*tatra*)—immediately thereafter, at that assembly, Śiśupāla, the lord of Cedi, could not endure the honor (*māna*), that is, the worship (*pūjā*), offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of the gods, by Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu.
In this regard, he states an arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by a general truth): "At the prosperity of others," etc.
*Matsarin* means envious or intolerant.
Now, [he speaks of] despondency (*viṣāda*).
But despondency, born from the absence of a means, is the depletion of one's vital strength; it causes sighing, gasping, distress in the heart, and the seeking out of companions. (VisSd 3.167)
As it was said by me: "This braid of yours, bound with a mass of curly hair, O friend, when it falls upon my breast, it crushes my heart like a black cobra that has been provoked."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) The exhaustion of sentient beings is the loss of power;
it differs from dejection because it arises from the absence of skillful means.
"This is 'Kuṭilā'—" "O friend! This braid of yours, bound with a mass of curling hair, tears and bites my heart like a staff of iron, like a black female serpent."
Thus is the Sanskrit.
Having seen a woman whose husband is away from home with her braided hair tied up, this is the speech of a female friend expressing despondency.
The "staff of exertion" (*āyāsayaṣṭi*) is the simile for tearing apart.
And at the bite, there is the black female serpent.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) "Eṣeti"—this braid of yours, my friend, is bound with a mass of curly, thick hair.
It tears and bites the heart like an iron rod or like a black female serpent.
Now, as for fortitude (*dhṛti*): fortitude is the state of having one's desires completely fulfilled through the attainment of desired knowledge and so forth.
It consists of the joy of speech regarding satiety, laughter, inspired eloquence, and so forth.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) "Jñāna" means satisfaction or satiety. As it says in my own [work]:
“Having oppressed the wretched among my own kin, having engaged in verbal strife, and having failed to consider even the most grievous torments of the afterlife that await me in the long run—
I have indeed accumulated floods of wealth for whose sake this very body, alas, has now found its true purpose in a mere handful of wild rice.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, sa) "Having performed [acts such as] the oppression of the wretched for the sake of this body..."—this is the speech of one who has become dispassionate toward *saṃsāra* and resides in a penance grove.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "For the sake of this body, I have accumulated heaps of wealth by performing the oppression of the wretched and so forth; yet now, this very body is indeed fulfilled even with a mere handful of wild rice (*nīvāra*)."
"Among one's own people" means among beloved ones; "verbal strife" means quarreling with words; "pertaining to the hereafter" means pertaining to the next world;
"long-standing" means lasting for a long time.
Now, regarding fickleness:
Fickleness is instability arising from envy, hatred, passion, and so forth;
in that state, there are such things as scolding, harshness, and acting according to one's own whims. (VisSd 3.169)
For example:
"O bee, for now, divert your restless mind toward other flower-creepers that can endure being crushed."
"Why do you pointlessly torment this innocent jasmine bud, which has not yet produced pollen, out of season?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) "In others"—O bee!
divert your restless mind among other flowering creepers, those flower-vines capable of withstanding being crushed.
"Why do you pointlessly torment the bud of the *navamālikā* out of season? What kind of girl is she—innocent and foolish, meaning one who is unable to endure being crushed?
She is one whose menses have not yet appeared and whose [menstrual] flow has not begun.
By the power of *samāsokti* (synecdoche/metaphorical identification), there is the perception of a hero tormenting a newly-wed bride.
Here, "one whose dust has not arisen" means one who is free from the association with passion (*rajas*).
Here, there is the fickleness (*capalatā*) of both the bee, which is the expressed meaning (*vācya*), and the hero, who is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Now, dejection (*glāni*):
Fatigue, arising from sexual pleasure, exertion, mental distress, hunger, thirst, and so forth, produces a lack of vitality, emaciation, and a lack of enthusiasm. (VisSd 3.170)
For example:

"A harsh and long-lasting grief, which withers the flower of her heart, causes her body—already pale and emaciated—to languish like a tender sprout severed from its bond; it is like the autumnal heat that withers the inner leaf of a *ketakī* flower."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kṣa) "Due to the exhaustion of passion"—this refers to a lack of vitality and a loss of strength.
The distinction between dejection (*dainya*) and despondency (*viṣāda*) lies in their being produced by specific causes.
"Like a young sprout":
her cruel and long-lasting grief withers her body, making it emaciated, wasted, and pale;
regarding this, he provides a simile.
Regarding "like a sprout" (*kisalayamiva*): [it means] from the bond, that is, the stalk.
Locanā:
(lo, e) Regarding "like a sprout"—the compound *śaradija* is a *aluk* compound.
Now, regarding reflection (cintā): reflection is meditation; it arises from the failure to attain what is beneficial and causes distress through the realization of emptiness.
As it says in my [work]:
“O fair-faced one, with your face resting in your palms, you seem to be uniting the blooming lotus with the moon’s orb, its rival; why do you ponder thus with your heart hidden within?”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) "By means of the lotus" (*kamalena*) means: "Uniting the blooming lotus with its adversary, the lunar orb."
O fair-faced one, with your face resting in the palm of your hand, what are you thinking? Your heart is placed within [her].
Thus is the Sanskrit.
Here, the palm of the hand is a blossoming lotus, and the face is the orb of the moon;
this is the heroine’s reflection.
Locanā:
(lo, ai) “By ‘with a lotus’— ‘O fair-faced one, with your face resting upon the palm of your hand, what are you thinking as you join the opposing lunar orb with a blooming lotus?’”
"With my heart placed within."
Now, as for reasoning (tarka): reasoning is inquiry; it is the dancer of the eyebrows, the head, and the fingers arising from doubt.
For example:
"Was he obstructed by his beloved? and so forth.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, kha) "Is he detained?"—this is an example of the state of longing due to separation (*virahotkaṇṭhitā*).

Regarding the statement that these are the thirty-three varieties of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribheda*), he says that this is merely an illustration: *Locanā*: [Commentary] The phrase "is he detained? is an example of the transitory emotion of longing due to separation (*virahotkaṇṭhitā*). As for the claim that there are thirty-three varieties of transitory emotions, he states that this is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is because, according to the *Bhāvaprakāśana*, there are forty-nine transitory emotions; furthermore, the *Rasārṇavasudhākara* enumerates fifty-one. Thus, the number thirty-three is not exhaustive. Among these, the following are considered primary: the eight beginning with love (*rati*) and the three beginning with wonder (*vismaya*). The remaining thirty-two are secondary. Among these, those such as dejection (*glāni*) and languor (*ālasya*) are considered subordinate to others. For instance, dejection is subordinate to sorrow (*śoka*), while languor is subordinate to fear (*bhaya*). Similarly, the two types of intoxication (*mada*)—that caused by wine and that caused by youth—are each subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of agitation (*autsukya*)—that arising from desire and that arising from fear—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of recollection (*smṛti*)—that arising from joy and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of forgetfulness (*vismṛti*)—that arising from joy and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of distraction (*cintā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of apprehension (*śaṅkā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of envy (*asūyā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of dissimulation (*avahittha*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of concealment (*gūḍhokti*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of modesty (*lajjā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of bashfulness (*vrīḍā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of pride (*garva*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of arrogance (*māna*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of self-deprecation (*svātmanindā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of self-praise (*ātmapraśaṃsā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of self-reproach (*ātmagarhaṇā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of self-accusation (*ātmābhiśaṃsana*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of self-blame (*ātmaparibhava*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of self-disparagement (*ātmanindā*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of self-contempt (*ātmaparibhava*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Furthermore, the two types of self-humiliation (*ātmaparibhava*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Similarly, the two types of self-abasement (*ātmanikṛti*)—that arising from desire and that arising from grief—are subordinate to one another. Likewise, the two types of self-surrender (*ātmaparāyaṇatā*)—that arising from desire and
"And these" refers to the following: these examples are intended solely to demonstrate the actual existence of the nature of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*).

Whether they are predominant in some instances or non-predominant in others, there is no impairment to the aesthetic experience (*pratīti*). Furthermore, even emotions such as love (*rati*) may function as transitory states within an indeterminate rasa.

For instance—in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), because it persists without being interrupted, *rati* (love) alone is denoted by the term "permanent emotion" (*sthāyibhāva*); whereas *hasa* (laughter), arising again and again, is merely a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), as it does not conform to the definition of a permanent emotion.
Thus it has been said:
“The supreme emotion (bhāva), when in the state of rasa, attains the status of the permanent emotion (sthāyin).
Thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.
"Even love and the others"—meaning those emotions which are fixed as *sthāyibhāvas* (permanent moods), when they become distinct from that state and are unfixed;
"characterized by transience" (*vyabhicārilakṣaṇa*)—because the definition of such [transient moods] consists in their occasional nature, characterized by rising and sinking [in intensity].
He shows the agreement here that even a *sthāyibhāva* becomes a *vyabhicāribhāva* (transient mood) in this context, stating: "in the state of rasa."
A *bhāva* such as love (*rati*) and so forth attains the status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) only when it exists solely as that very *rasa* at a later stage;
however, from the force of the word "only" (*eva*), it is understood that one not in such a state does not attain the status of a permanent emotion.
Furthermore, one not in such a state can only exist as another *rasa*.

And if that [transitory state] is helpful there [to the dominant emotion], then because it moves directly toward what persists in that [emotion], it is pervaded by the definition of a transitory state; thus, since the word "transitory" (*vyabhicārin*) possesses both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*) therein, it too becomes a transitory state.
It should be understood that this relationship has been shown with the intention of conveying this meaning as obtained through the force of the context.
To the question, "For which permanent emotion (sthāyin) and in which rasa is [which transitory emotion] considered a transitory one (sañcārin)?", he says:
Laughter is held to belong to the erotic and the heroic rasas; likewise, anger is held to belong to the heroic. (Viśvavidyā 3.172)
"Disgust is said [to occur] even in the peaceful [rasa] as a transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva)," and so forth;
other such points should be inferred by those whose intellects have been cultivated accordingly.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, gha) Other points such as these are to be inferred accordingly. For this very reason, in the verse beginning "He who took away my childhood" (*kaumārahara*), the wonder (*vismaya*)—which is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhutarasā*)—functions as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
However, according to the author's own view, that verse is an illustration specifically of the suggestion of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāvadhvani*).

Indeed, from the commentary on the passage in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* stating "because of the primacy of rasa alone," it is understood that the word *rasa* refers to the transitory moods (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Now, as for the permanent mood (*sthāyibhāva*):
it is that which neither compatible nor incompatible [moods] are able to obscure.
This state, which is the bulbous root for the sprout of relish, is recognized as the stable emotional tone (sthāyin).
Vijñapriyā:

"Whether non-contradictory or contradictory"—this means that the transitory moods (*avyabhicāribhāva*) are either non-contradictory or contradictory to the dominant mood (*sthāyibhāva*). "To conceal" means to render [them] outside the range of the intellect.
As it has been said:
"Like a thread passing through pearls, the permanent emotion (sthāyin) follows other emotions; it is not concealed by them, but rather is nourished by them to the highest degree."
Thus [ends the section]. *Vijñapriyā*:
"By means of the commentary on the *Straksūtra*."

The *sthāyibhāva* (the permanent emotion) is that which follows and is connected with the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory emotions); it is not concealed by those states, meaning it does not become an object outside of cognition.
To illustrate this quality of following along, he says "like the thread of a garland" (*srag-sūtra*).
According to the method of usage, just as in a flower garland the thread is necessarily connected [to all the flowers], such is the meaning.
To the question of what kind [of state] is produced by those [factors] connected with itself, he says: "by them, this...
The meaning is that it is nourished, i.e., it is made to sprout as the taste (*āsvāda*).
— *Locanā*:
(La, Au) "Now" (*atha*) [introduces] the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which has reached its turn according to the order of enumeration.
"Non-contradictory" (*aviruddha*)... [etc.]
In the poems of great poets, the non-obscuration of the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) by even contradictory [emotions] is indeed clearly manifested.
Regarding the word "garland" (*sraj*): the meaning is that it remains as something that runs through all the flowers or pearls, like a string (*sūtra*).
By those states [of emotion].
He states their subdivisions:
"Love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, and likewise fear,"
In this way, disgust, wonder, and tranquility are also said to be eight. (VisSd 3.175)
Locanā:
(lo, a) Regarding the rasa of tranquility (*śānti*), whose dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is peace (*śama*), there is a separate mention of it as the ninth because it is new;
therein—
Rati (love) is the inclination of the mind toward an object agreeable to it;
hāsa (laughter) is held to be the expansion of the heart through distortions of speech and other such expressions.

The mental despondency resulting from the loss of what is desired and so forth is designated by the term "sorrow" (śoka). The perception of sharpness toward disagreeable objects is held to be "anger" (krodha).
Vigour in the commencement of undertakings is called steadfast enthusiasm;
whereas fear is the agitation of the mind produced by the power of the terrible (raudra).
Censure arises from the perception of faults and so forth, while disgust is born of wonder regarding various objects that transcend the limits of worldly experience. (VisSd 3.179)
The expansion of the mind is declared to be wonder;
tranquility is the bliss born from resting in one's own self within a state of effortless abiding.
For example, love in the *Mālatīmādhava*; laughter in the *Laṭakamelaka*;
and sorrow in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
In the *Mahābhārata*, there is tranquility (*śama*);
likewise elsewhere as well.

For these [emotions], arising within those [stable emotions] through various states—both contradictory and non-contradictory—are not interrupted, but rather are fully nourished, as established by the experience of sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
Vijñapriyā: (vi, cha) "Rati" and so forth;
"pravaṇāyita" means an intense immersion.
And that [smiling] culminates in affection alone.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "speech etc.," the inclusion of dress is intended.

The expansion of the mind is a cognition produced by a particular conjunction of the mind, which culminates in the cognition of being an object of ridicule, from which a smile arises in the form of the expansion of the face.
*Vaiklavya* is a particular kind of suffering;
*saṃrambha* is impetuosity accompanied by joy;
*stheyān* means stable or enduring.
The cognition of sharpness arises from the intense desire to retaliate. The "fierce" one is capable of inflicting harm;
through his power—that is, his capacity—there is a deficiency which serves as the cause for fleeing due to the knowledge of future suffering.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the perception of defects, etc."—*doṣa* refers to distorted sounds and so forth; by the word "etc. (*ādibhiḥ*), the inclusion of the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is intended.
*Gārhā* means censure.
*Vismayodbhavā* means arising from wonder.

"How can he have such a fault?"— thus, the expansion of the mind produced by wonder is the investigation of causes through the knowledge that [the fault] is impossible given the perceived causes. "Resting in the self" is knowledge whose object is the self alone.
"In these" means when these [factors] such as *rati* (love) and so forth exist.
He states the etymological derivation of the term "state" (*bhāva*) for the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), and the rest:
Locanā:
(lo, ā) "Rati" and so forth;
"pravaṇāyitam" means the state of being inclined.
This *rati* (erotic sentiment), when possessed by passion (*madana*),

is exclusively directed toward a woman or a man; it is the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), for otherwise it would not conform to the definition of a permanent emotion.
In these passages just mentioned,
furthermore:
because they cultivate the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) through their connection with various modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya).
Therefore, these states are declared to be the stable emotions (sthāyin), the transitory emotions (saṃcārī), and the involuntary emotions (sāttvika).
As it has been said:
"The state [of the self] is the cultivation of that state through entities such as pleasure, pain, and so forth."—
*Vijñapriyā*.
(VI, JA) "Furthermore" means:
they bring about [the experience] or make known [it] by means of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

The cultivation (*bhāvana*)—that is, the awakening—of that state, namely the existence of *rasa* such as love (*rati*), by means of states such as pleasure and pain; therefore, the meaning is that love and so forth are the *bhāvas*.
Locanā:
(lo, i) "Pleasure," etc.

Through emotions—whether residing in oneself or residing in the poem—one contemplates, hears, or sees the emotion, that is, the essential nature, of that character to be imitated, such as Rāma and others.
Now, he states the divisions of rasa: "The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, and the terrifying..."
The loathsome, the marvelous—thus eight flavors are recognized, as well as the peaceful.
Locanā: (lo,
ī) With the words "Now" (*atha*), she sets out to define the essential nature of rasa, along with its adjuncts, according to the direction already indicated.

Eight [rasas] were explicitly mentioned by the Great Sage (Maharṣi) as being based on dramatic performance (*abhinaya*), which consists of imitating the narratives of the Purāṇas preceded by songs and instrumental music abounding in *sattva*.

Regarding the fact that there is also a ninth rasa, the *śānta* (the peaceful), in works to be heard such as the *mahākāvya*, its separate mention is not entirely correct because it lacks utility for drama.
As Dhanika said: "There is no nourishment (*puṣṭi*) for this [śānta] in dramas."
And thus, because it is characterized by the relish of unsurpassed bliss, the view of those who maintain that there is only a single rasa and no distinctions is also refuted.

For this very reason it has been said: “The causes, the effects, those which may be variable, and the essential nature itself—it is from the existence of these that the distinctions of *śṛṅgāra* and the other rasas are traditionally known.”

Among these, the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*): "For *śṛṅga* is the arousal of passion; the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that has as its cause the arrival of that [arousal] and which primarily belongs to characters of superior nature is recognized as the erotic. (VisSd 3.183)
Excluding a woman already married and a courtesan who lacks passion, the heroines may serve as the objects of attachment, as may the heroes such as the *dakṣiṇa* and others. (VisSd 3.184)
The moon, sandalwood, the *narolamba* bird, sounds, and so forth, are considered the excitants (*uddīpana*);
the movement of the eyebrows, side-long glances, and so forth, are proclaimed to be the ensuants (*anubhāva*). (VisSd 3.185)
Having abandoned ferocity, death, indolence, disgust, and infidelity, its permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is love (*rati*); it is dark-complexioned and has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, jha) "Having as its cause the arrival of that" means: the arrival or attainment of Manmatha (the god of love) is itself the cause of such [a state],
occurring specifically in those who possess desire due to the arousal of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
"And a prostitute" (veśyām) means one who has not been married; for in the case of one who has been married,
[the status of] being "married to another" already applies.
In this way, one's own wife and daughter are likewise [of four types].
"Dakṣiṇā and so forth" means those who are clever (dakṣiṇa), bold (dhṛṣṭa), compliant (anukūla), and deceitful (śaṭha).

And those very bees (*rolamba*) are the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), just as a woman married to another is for the sentiment of the heroic (*vīra*); however, in the case of the fierce sentiment (*raudra*),
there is a renunciation of that [beauty].
Since it is precisely the *sambhoga* [stage] that is to be described for one who has just reached the state of being born—that is, death—it is the actual death itself that is abandoned.
Locanā:
(lo, u) "The peak"—this is another name for the peak of the emergence of passion (*manmatha*).
Its "arrival" (*āgamanam*) refers to its manifestation within *ramā* and the other [objects].

Since the word *āra* is derived from the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go") preceded by the prefix *ā*, and since the specific emergence of passion (*manmatha*) is indicated therein, it is suggested that this [passion] is caused by the exceedingly mature mutual affection between both the woman and the man who constitute the primary substrata of this *rasa*.
For it will be stated that when passion (*anurāga*) is fixed upon a single object, there is a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
There are four types, beginning with the *dakṣiṇa*.

Regarding these rasas, the description of their colors and deities is set aside in the context of plays and similar works—those intended to ensure the absence of obstacles—and in the worship and other rites performed by actors.
He explains this with the words "here," and so forth.
Here, [the excitant cause] has been shown only partially;
it should be understood in detail from the first chapter.
For example: "The dwelling is empty," and so forth.
Here, the Lord is of the nature described therein.
The young woman, whose nature has been described, constitutes the objective determinant (ālambana-vibhāva) and the excitant determinant (ālambana-vibhāva).
The empty bedchamber is the excitant determinant (uddīpana-vibhāva).
The kiss is the consequent (anubhāva).
Shame and laughter are transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*).

When the emotion of love (*rati-bhāva*) is manifested through these, it becomes the object of experience for those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) and assumes the form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). He states its divisions as follows:
Separation and union—thus this [love] is considered to be of two kinds.
In this regard—
where there is intense passion, yet the desired object is not attained, that is *vipralambha* (love-in-separation);
[the desired object being] either the hero (*nāyaka*) or the heroine (*nāyikā*).
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ña) "He does not attain what is desired"— the heroine is desired by the hero, and the hero is desired by the heroine.
And "desirability" (abhīṣṭatā) consists in being favorable.
Therefore, even when favorability has been attained toward a proud woman, for the hero there is only *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
— *Locanā*:

Regarding the phrase "But where" (*yatra tu*): *rati* is defined as longing; when it reaches its highest intensity, if that excellence of passion does not reach the heroine from the perspective of the hero, nor the hero from the perspective of the heroine, this is the meaning.
And that is *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
Furthermore, it is of four kinds: consisting of first love (*pūrvarāga*), jealousy (*māna*), separation (*pravāsa*), and sorrow (*karuṇa*). (VisSd 3.187)
In that regard:

"When two people have developed mutual passion through either hearing of or seeing one another, that particular state which exists before their union is called *pūrvarāga* (preliminary passion). (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 3.188)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) "That which is produced" is the ellipsis for "a particular state. A particular state refers to the ten stages occurring during the period of separation.
The singular number in the word "viśeṣa" (distinction) is used by relying on the unity of the nature of distinction.
"Pūrvarāga" (preliminary passion) is passion prior to the attainment of the desired object.
Since it has been stated that this arises either from hearing or from seeing, he states the means for both hearing and seeing:

In that regard, hearing [of the deity] may occur through the mouths of messengers, captive women, or female companions; while seeing [the deity] occurs through a magical illusion, a painting, or directly in a dream. (VisSd 3.189)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) "But hearing" (śravaṇam tu)—this means hearing from the mouth of a messenger or others, or seeing with the eyes through [the illusions of] a magic show or a dream.
Here, the word "directly" (sākṣāt) refers ultimately to the eye which is the cause thereof.
Longing, reflection, remembrance, recounting of virtues, agitation, lamentation,
madness, disease, stupor, and death— these are the ten stages of love in this world.
Longing is desire; anxiety is the thinking of means for attainment and so forth;
and madness is the lack of discrimination even regarding what is sentient and insentient. (VisSd 3.191)
Due to the intense wandering of the mind, there may be incoherent speech that cannot be discerned;
furthermore, there will be diseases such as long-drawn sighing, pallor, emaciation, and so forth.
Inertness is the lack of movement in the limbs as well as in the mind.
Vijñapriyā (vi, ḍa):
"Non-discrimination even regarding sentient and insentient things"—the meaning is the failure to discriminate between sentience and so forth.
Therefore, because trees and the like lack consciousness and thus cannot form a connection [of meaning], the statement is one of cowardice.
Since *saṃlāpa* (discourse) is a synonym for *pralāpa* (incoherent speech), he states the definition of *pralāpa*: "without a basis" (*alakṣya*).
This refers to speech directed toward that which lacks a basis, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) that includes even meaningless speech; likewise, it should be understood that what was previously stated as "long sighs" and so forth, as well as "due to illness, fever," and the like, is included by the word "etcetera" (ādi) here.
The rest is clear.
The examples in sequence are as follows:
“May those various gestures of the lovely-eyed one—moist with love, touching upon affection, arising from familiarity and the dawning of intense passion, and naturally sweet—be directed toward me.”
In which [arts], even when merely imagined through desire, there occurs for the internal organ an absorption dense with bliss that instantly obstructs the activity of the external organs.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) "Moist with love"—this is Mādhava’s speech.
May such various, extraordinary gestures of Mālatī’s face-beholdings manifest toward me.
The qualifiers of the gestures are "moist with love" and so forth.
Moistness consists in being as if wet due to a lack of stillness;
affection is tenderness.
The meaning is that these indicate that. "Familiarity" (paricaya) means seeing [them] repeatedly.

In whatever activities—though they be merely imagined through hope or desire—the dissolution (laya), which is a state of absorption (līnatā) thickly pervaded by the bliss of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), occurs in an instant.

The meaning is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes pervaded by bliss. Of what nature is this dissolution (*laya*)? It is the obstructer, that is, the hinderer, of the activity of the external organs.
Here, through the medium of vision, movement, and longing, there is a desire directed toward Mālatī alone.
Locanā:

Regarding "moist with love" (*premārdrā*)—*prema* (love) is a particular state of mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) that manifests an internal disposition (*bhāva*) directed toward seeing [the beloved] and so forth; *praṇaya* (affection) is subjugation preceded by that [love];
and *paricaya* (intimacy) is the sharing of secrets.
Absorption (*laya*) is indeed the state of being identical with that [object].
Here, Mādhava, whose passion has taken root from the direct sight of Mālatī, feels a longing:
"How can I behold the deer-eyed one, the very goddess Lakṣmī of the Mind-born God?"
Thus, his beloved, agitated by such thoughts, does not find sleep throughout the night.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) The passage beginning with "How shall I look... is clear. It does not reach, that is, it does not pervade, the night.
Here, there is the reflection of a hero whose passion has grown intense from witnessing a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) regarding a certain heroine.
"This is mine"—
in such passages as "toward me with feignedness," there is the recollection of the hero.
In passages such as "eyes that surpass the khanjana bird," there is a description of qualities (*guṇa*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ta): In the passage beginning with "eyes," beauty itself is the quality.
In passages such as "he releases his breath," there is agitation (*udvega*).
And in the passage, "When three parts of the night remained, he closed his eyes and suddenly woke up;
where is Nīlakaṇṭha? [there is another].
"Go," she said with words unperceived, her arms cast around his neck in an embrace of falsehood.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
tha) "When one-third remains" refers to this speech addressed by Pārvatī’s friend Vijayā to Maheśa, while she was disguised in the attire of an ascetic.
Having remained awake for three parts of the night, she suddenly awoke while closing her eyes;
what was she like? She had placed the coils of her arms around the neck of the insincere Hara, crying out, "O Blue-throated One!
Where are you going?"—thus speaking words that were unperceived and without support.
In this context, there is *pralāpa* (incoherent speech).
In the verse beginning with "O brother, O *dvirepha*," there is *unmāda* (madness).
[The verse continues: "Your face is pale and emaciated, your heart is full of passion, and your body is languid."
"O friend, it announces within the heart a consumptive disease in its extreme form."
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) "Pāṇiḍvati"—a disease that is not to be cut [out] in another's field is a *kṣetriya* disease;
here, it refers to a chronic illness.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "pāṇḍukṣāmām" etc.—this is the speech of Lavaṅgikā, who is asking Mālatī about her state of separation.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O friend, [the state of] your heart's internal 'field-disease'—a disease in this field, namely the body, which is incurable—[is] the agent that makes known [your condition], such as a pale and emaciated face."
*Kṣāmaṃ* means emaciated;
*sarasaṃ* means moist with essence.
"Her entire body, placed upon the cool stone slab, is perfectly motionless."
This long-drawn sigh tells only this much: that he still lives.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) Regarding "the lotus-pond": "Though every limb placed upon the bed of lotus petals is motionless, this long burden of sighs alone proves that she is indeed alive."
Thus [is] the Sanskrit.
Every limb is motionless;
therefore, the meaning is that she lives and accomplishes [her purpose] through this very long sigh alone.
In this context, there is insentience;
"this is mine.
Death is not described at all because it would cause an interruption of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
If that which is about to be born, which is to be expressed, and which is thus desired by the mind,
were to be described even now, it would be as if one were reviving a corpse from nearby.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) "That which is desired by the mind"—the meaning is that only the longing for death is to be described, not death itself.
[The objection] "But it is also described" [is raised].
Furthermore, the meaning is that even death must be described when life is imminent.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Upon seeing the *śephālikā* flower in full bloom, the slender maiden was somehow able to sustain her life-breaths."
Having now heard the cry of the cock, I do not know what will become of that poor woman.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) "The *śephālikā*"—meaning it has been crushed, its flowers having fallen because of being crushed during the final portion of the night;
for perhaps even at that time, she maintains her life-breath with the hope of the hero's arrival.
The crowing of the cock-fighters occurs only at the time of dawn; this is a statement of despondency by her friend, anticipating death there. "Tapasvinī" means one who is suffering.
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) "The *śephālikā*"—by the mention of the *śephālikā* flower, the hour of midnight is indicated; "the ascetic woman" means she is to be pitied.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:
“Let the bees fill the quarters with the tumultuous din of their humming; let even the breeze born of the sandalwood groves approach very slowly;
let the intoxicated playful cuckoos on the tips of the mango trees take up the fifth note; and let these vital breaths, as hard as stone, depart—depart quickly!”
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, pha) *rolambā* means:
this is the speech of a heroine who has not yet obtained a sight of her leader."
Regarding the phrase "may they fulfill," "the green ones" is the object;
[it refers to] the green directions.
"The wind" is the breeze.
Let the cuckoos,
the pet kokilas,
the humming of bees, and so forth, serve as excitants for the time being.
The meaning is: "Let even these harsh breaths depart.
Let them reckon [the time] and sing.
Locanā:
"Lo, e! refers to bees; these two belong to me.
As for the third [example]:—
In the account of Mahāśvetā and Puṇḍarīka in the *Kādambarī*: "The third" means the third [occurrence], namely life after death.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) "The third" refers to the third [instance of] living following death.
And we shall explain that this type of *karuṇa* (pathos) pertains to the domain of *vipralambha* (separation).
Locanā:
(lo, ai) In the narrative of Mahāśvetā and Puṇḍarīka, Puṇḍarīka, having lost his life, regained it once again.
This is the domain of *karuṇavipralambha* (love-in-separation through grief),
and not of *pūrvarāga* (first love) or *pravāsa* (separation due to travel).
However, some [authorities] say—
“First there is the pleasure of the eyes, then attachment of the mind, and then the formation of mental constructs;
followed by the loss of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, and the destruction of shame.”
"Insanity, fainting, and death— these alone are the ten stages of love," so they say.
And therein:
"At first, the passion of the woman is to be expressed; that of the man [is to be inferred] afterwards by her gestures.
Locanā:
Regarding "at first"—the meaning is "having observed her gestures" (*tadiṅgitaiḥ*).

*Ingita* refers to gestures indicative of passion. These have been described right here [in the verse] beginning with, "Having seen him, she shows bashfulness," and so forth; thus the *ingitas* have been explained.
Just as in the *Ratnāvalī*, where the passion of the man for Sāgarikā and Vatsarāja becomes even more heart-wrenching at the outset, despite its very possibility;
thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, bha) Regarding the phrase "the gestures have been described"—this refers to the expression of passion itself.
First, he demonstrates the passion for women: "In the *Ratnāvalī*," etc.—herein lies the intense passion (*praganurāga*) of Sāgarikā.
"Nīlī, kusumbha, and mañjiṣṭhā; likewise, *pūrvarāga* (preliminary passion) is also threefold. (VisSd 3.195)
Locanā:
(lo, au) refers to the indigo dye, the blue dye, the safflower dye, and the madder dye; such is the meaning.
In that regard:
"That love which does not depart from the mind and yet does not shine intensely is called *nīlī-rāga* (indigo-dye love), such as that between Śrī Rāma and Sītā. (VisSd 3.196)
They call that the safflower dye which fades yet remains beautiful;
they call that the madder dye which does not fade and shines exceedingly.
Vijñapriyā:
"And it does not shine exceedingly" means that because it is indistinct, it does not shine exceedingly.

Regarding "of Śrī Rāma and Sītā": since Śrī Rāma is *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled), like Purūravas, he does not shine exceedingly due to the absence of excessive lamentation; this is the meaning.
Now, regarding pride (*māna*): pride is anger, and it is of two kinds, arising from love or from jealousy.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ya) Immediately following *pūrvarāga*, he describes *māna* (love-in-anger): "Now," etc.—meaning that which arises through either affection (*praṇaya*) or jealousy (*īrṣyā*). It is said: "Love-in-anger may occur between two [lovers] even when there is very great joy. (VisSd 3.198)
Because love follows a crooked course, there is anger without cause;
this [anger] belongs to both—the hero and the heroine—and the mutual affection of both should be described.
An example:
In that regard, as for the hero:
"O lover, with eyelids heavy with sleep and eyes closed, grant me an opportunity,
you whose limbs quiver at the touch of a kiss upon the cheek."
"I shall not delay any longer."
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ra) "O you who feign sleep"— O fortunate one, with eyes closed in feigned slumber, this is my opportunity.
My body is thrilled by the kissing of your cheeks; I shall not delay any longer.
Thus [ends] the Sanskrit. This is the heroine’s reply to the hero, who, while being loved, feigned sleep and kissed her; she was then praised by him. "O you who feign sleep!"
O you with closed eyes, O fortunate one!
By my kissing your cheek, your very body—meaning your body alone—is thrilled with horripilation; this is the space for me, the space for my own abiding.
Even now, because there is no manifestation [of them], their non-existence is certain;
therefore, the meaning is: "I shall not delay.
And in this regard, one should not suspect that the word *te* (you) is impossible according to the rule: "That which was previously addressed more than once... [Pāṇini 8.1.29].
Because the meaning of that [rule] is simply the non-existence of the vocative word immediately preceding;
however, after a vocative word preceded by *upa*, the substitute *te* and so forth certainly do occur.
— Locanā:
*Lo-a*: "Māna" means not having reached the stage of formal instruction;
"praṇaya" means affection; "alia" means [a friend].
O you who have given birth falsely!
O you with closing eyes!
Give, O fortunate one!
Make way for me;
my limbs are bristling with thrill from the kiss upon your cheek,
so I shall not tarry any longer.
This is the speech of the heroine, who, after the hero—who had been feigning sleep while covering the entire bed—had kissed her cheek as she lingered for some time;
it occurs, for example, in the *Kumārasambhava* during the description of the twilight.
*Vijñapriyā*: [The verse follows].
(vi, la) Regarding the *Kumārasambhava*:

here, when Maheśa had departed to perform his twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), leaving Pārvatī behind, and while Pārvatī was engaged in her indignation (*māna*) and the subsequent effort to break it, [the poet describes] that body which, O fair-limbed one, was previously abandoned by Saṃdhyā— the daughter of Kamalayoni— [at the time of her own departure].
Since she, O proud lady, resorts to both setting and rising, for that reason I hold her in high esteem here.
Thus it is stated in the teachings of Maheśa.
As for both [the lover and the beloved], it is said:
"Of two lovers who have quarreled, who are lying on their sides with their faces turned away from each other, and who are full of pride..."
"Who is the wrestler against those who have bestowed their command by means of still and restrained breath?"
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
va) “When two lovers, pretending to be asleep while actually feigning anger, are both intent on testing each other’s pride—
with their breath held motionless and their ears strained for sound— who is the victor?”
“Thus, who is a refined person? Who is a wrestler capable of protecting his pride?
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā)—“It is the gambler (*paṇatra*).”
“Between two lovers who are both feigning sleep out of pride, yet are angry with one another,
and who have stilled their breath and pressed their ears close to listen— who is the victor?”

The sense here is that it is not known who the wrestler is, nor who is capable of enduring him for long. However, if he is unable to endure the ultimate conciliation, this does not constitute a variety of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation),
but rather the state of the transitory emotion (*sañcārībhāva*) called *sambhoga* (enjoyment).
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, śa) *na vipralambhabhedatā* means "not a variety of *vipralambha*" [love-in-separation]. This is a statement by a female friend to a heroine who is unable to maintain her pride during the knitting of her brows.
For example:

"Though a frown is fashioned, her gaze looks up with even greater longing; though her speech is restrained, this wretched face breaks into a smile; though her heart has been made stern, her body takes on a thrill of horripilation—when that person is seen, how can there be a conclusion to my pride?"
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṣa) "Even when I knit my brows, my gaze looks longingly at that beloved"—in this manner, when that most beloved person is seen, how can there be the fulfillment or maintenance of pride? This is the syntactical connection.
"My face is scorched and my countenance is censured.
Or, for example:
"On a single bed, they lay with their backs turned to one another and suffered in silence; though a conciliation resided in each other's hearts, they both guarded their pride."
As the eyes of the couple mingled through the gradual movement of their sidelong glances, the strife of pride was broken by a passionate embrace, swift with laughter.
When the union of one's own beloved with another man is seen, inferred, or heard; ||| VisSd_3.199 ||

Envy and pride may arise in women; in that regard, there are three types of inference based on the occurrence of snoring during sleep, marks of sexual enjoyment, and the slippage of one's family name.
Locanā:
(lo, i) "By envy"—this refers to its being a transitory emotion (*bhāva*) known as envy, due to its connection with the definition of a transitory state.
"As if dreaming" (*utsvapnāyitam*)—the term *utsvapnāyita* means activity within a dream.
Arising at the very moment of waking from sleep in order to speak of that;
stumbling over a name while addressing someone, which results in uttering that person's name;
and therein, as seen in the following example:
"O beloved, with the breath from her face, she removes the pollen from the eyes of Sudṛśā;
meanwhile, the two eyes of that rival young woman are repeatedly filled with the dust of anger."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, sa) *Utsvapnāyitam* is the vision in a dream of one's husband’s union with another woman.
As in my [work]: “O friend!...”
"What do you say? 'My husband is not devoted to anyone other than me; he is a rogue, and you, being straightforward, do not know him. [I reply:
'In a dream, I saw him leaving the ocean palace and intent on union with another young woman. Therefore, enough with this talk of affection.'"
He provides an illustration regarding the sight of one's husband in the company of another beloved woman: "She restrains" [the glance].
This refers to the glance of a beautiful-eyed woman who is a co-wife;
it is the pride born of jealousy.
An example of inference through the signs of enjoyment is as follows:
“You hide your body with its fresh nail-marks behind your garment, and you again cover with your hand your lip bitten by teeth;
yet how can this pervasive fragrance of wine, spreading in every direction and proclaiming your union with another woman, be concealed?”
The same applies to other cases as well.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ha) Regarding "not new": although you may be able to conceal [the marks] such as nail-prints left by union with another heroine by means of fresh garments and the like, nevertheless, by what means can the fragrance of the body-unguents from that amorous friction be hidden?
The meaning of the sentence is that it is possible to prevent [it].
"In the same way elsewhere" refers to what has already been illustrated regarding the state of dreaming while awake (*utsvapnāyita*).

Regarding a slip of the tongue (*gotraskhalita*), as for example: "On a single bed, while the charming girl lay with her face turned away in sudden anger because she perceived the presence of rival women, her beloved—though offering endearments—was ignored by her out of agitation. Remaining silent, he was then, at that very moment, looked upon again with her neck gracefully turned, lest he should seem as if he had fallen asleep."
Or as it is said by me:
"O friend, whatever endearments he, who is attached to another woman, performs toward me, know for certain that all of this is surely feigned affection."
Then, while meditating upon her, that gambler indeed used to address me in secret during our playtime, repeatedly calling me by her name.
"Thus:
conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, intimidation, and indifference are the other means;
the husband should employ these six expedients in sequence to break her [resistance]. (VisSd 3.201)
In that regard, conciliation (*sāma*) consists of pleasant speech; sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the winning over of their friends;
bribery (*dāna*) is the offering of ornaments and such under a pretext; and prostration (*nati*) is falling at their feet. (VisSd 3.202)
But when the *sāma* (conciliation) and other [means] have been exhausted, there may be disregard through indifference;
or, from impetuosity, fear, joy, and so forth, there may be a lapse of anger into another rasa.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kṣa) "Natyupekṣe" means "bowing and equanimity.
That is, *nati* and *upekṣā*.
"That which can be acquired" means the acquisition or winning over of that proud woman's friend.
"Giving by means of a pretext" means the giving of ornaments and so forth.
In this context, with reference to the single category of "giving" (*dāna*), there are two types to be observed:
