Here, by virtue of the plural number, it is understood that for the unattached heroine—the courtesan—there is a plurality of lovers.
"The King of Vatsa," it is said.
In this context, the reading "of Vatsarāja" is in some places unauthentic.
An example of [the sentiment] residing in a rival protagonist (*pratināyaka*) is found in the description of Hayagrīva’s water-sports during the slaying of Hayagrīva.
An example of its presence in a low-ranking character (*adhamapātra*) is as follows:

A certain Bhilla woman, whose hips were adorned with leafy creepers and who was like a mountain jasmine flower upon the earth, having gathered flowers on the mountain and sitting before her husband, had her own hair combed by him.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) "On her hips"—like a certain Bhilla woman, a Kirāti, who had bound or worn a leafy creeper (*patravallī*) upon her hips;

having gathered *girimallī* flowers—that is, *kuṭaja* blossoms—while sitting before him on the mountain, she had her hair, by means of her own husband (her servant), literally "up-pulled" with the gathered flowers, meaning she caused it to be made radiant.
This is a form derived from the verbal root *cad*, which has the meaning "to shine.
Furthermore, in the word *vallī*, this is the form of the stem *vallī* ending in a short vowel;
for if it ended in a long vowel, the suffix *ka* would have been required.
In this context, there is the longing for an inferior husband,
as when [a woman] is among animals and so forth— for example:
"Calling her beloved amidst the forest thickets, she calls out to him from within the creepers among the finest jasmine plants."
The female bee took up the melody of the song consisting of the modulations of the warbling of the moving five-stringed lute.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) Regarding the phrase "among the *mallīmatallīs*": *matallī* is a specific type of flower.
The meaning is "standing within the valley.

"A concert consisting of the melodic modulations of the sound of a lute" refers to the concert produced by the melodic modulations of the sound of a *vipañcī*—that is, a lute (*vīṇā*)—which is shimmering.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), ascetics and others are included.

An example of one appearing fierce (*raudrābhāsa*) is as follows: “With wide, rolling eyes red and dilated, his limbs trembling violently, casting aside his ear (as if in defiance), and free from fear, Arjuna—holding his bow and arrows while Hara looked on—repeatedly proclaimed his own prowess in battle with bitter words; then, expert at slapping his arms, he entered to slay Yudhiṣṭhira.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "The ascetic and others"—
here, it should be understood as referring to the passion of King Jīmūtavāhana, the ascetic, for Malayavatī.

Regarding the verse beginning with *raktotphulla*: Arjuna, provoked by the bitter words of Yudhiṣṭhira who had suffered humiliation from Karṇa’s ear, became enraged and, abandoning Karṇa while he was still fighting, set out to kill Yudhiṣṭhira.

The phrase *apetabhīr hareḥ paśyataḥ* means "fearless, devoid of the fear of slaying his elder"—that is, disregarding Hari (Kṛṣṇa) as he looked on; here, the genitive case (*hareḥ*) is used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*).
*Sva* means one's own.
*Aṃsa* is the shoulder;
he is skillful (*paṭu*) in slapping (*āsphoṭe*) it.

It has not been cited [as an example] in cases of the *hāsya* (comic) rasa based on inferior objects such as a teacher, nor in the *vīra* (heroic) rasa when directed toward a base object, such as the exertion for killing a Brahmin or similar acts.
This is shown in order: "Having obtained birth here in a Caṇḍāla womb, even the birth of a twice-born is no longer desired by me.
Somewhere in a holy forest, casting off this body, I aspire to the severance of rebirth. (1)
Constantly releasing downward breath, his hair disheveled and unkempt,
his mouth smeared with saliva and his garments soiled with filth— may this teacher of mine always instruct me.
For my arrows, whose thirst has not been quenched by the blood of minor heroes, shall today find satisfaction in the blood of Droṇa. // 3 //
These Kirātas, with their bows bristling with arrows, have set out at full speed to capture the deer they pierced; seeing him, they run after the sons of the king as if he were but a blade of grass.
An example of the appearance of the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) is as follows:
"Unable to endure the sight of him, as if it were that of the thousand-rayed sun,
the owl of timid eyes entered the interior of a cave-dwelling on the Golden Mountain and spent his days in fear."
Vijñapriyā:

"Unable to..."—Kauśika Vāsava, being unable to endure the sight of that asura who possessed a thousand smiles, entered a cave in the Golden Mountain (*Hemādri*) out of fear and passed his days there. *Adhīralocanaḥ* means one with timid and tremulous eyes.
This is an instance of the suggested simile (upamādhvani) rooted in the power of words (śabdaśaktimūla).

For instance, the owl (pecaka), being of unsteady intellect and sightless due to blindness by day, is unable to endure the sight of the thousand-rayed sun; thus, having entered a mountain cave, it passes its days.
And thus, in the phrase "like Indra [is] a blind man," there is the suggestion of a simile (*upamā-dhvani*).
Here, this should be noted:
it will be explained later that rasa, bhāva, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and so forth, constitute suggestion where the sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).
And that [is so] precisely because there is no perception of the sequence of manifestation for the underlying emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) which is to be manifested.
In this verse, since the underlying emotion of fear (*bhaya*) is expressed by the word "fearing" (*bibhyat*), it lacks the status of being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*);

how then could there be a non-manifestedness (*asaṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgyatva*) dependent on the non-perception of a sequence of manifestation? Therefore, this is not a *dhvani* of the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
However, this is indeed a path of metaphor (upamādhvani).
An example of it is: "That King Kālayavana was praiseworthy even though he was flawed by his birth;
for upon seeing him prepared for battle, even Śrī Kṛṣṇa fled."
For fear, which has women and low persons as its object, is the very nature of the rasa;
the same applies elsewhere.
However, the semblance of emotion (bhāvābhāsa) may occur in relation to objects such as prostitutes with respect to [emotions] like shame.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) Regarding the subject of courtesans and the like;

as in the case of one who resides among courtesans and so forth—her face bowed in playfulness, drawing down the cloth from her head and bringing it forward, she drinks in the minds of the youths on all sides with glances from the corners of her eyes.
O friend, have you not seen a courtesan?
By the merit of some fortunate soul, she proceeds with her supreme grace to cause the flood of his merit to reach its full fruition.
In this case, the state of being mixed with the modesty of a courtesan is clear.
[This occurs] respectively when there is the subsidence (śānti) of one emotion (bhāva), or its emergence (udaya), or when two emotions are in conjunction (saṃdhi) or mixture (miśrita).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) *Sandhi* is the blending of successive contradictory states; that itself is *śabalatā* (variegation).
In that case, because each subsequent state is stronger in relation to each preceding one,
whereas a *sandhi* (euphonic junction) occurs when two elements are of equal status; thus,
"sutanu" is clear.
The quiescence, arising, conjunction, and variegation of an entity are thus considered.
For example, in sequence:
"O fair-limbed one, abandon your anger; look at me prostrate at your feet. Indeed, never before has your anger been of such a kind.
When the lord spoke thus, she, with her eyes cast askance and half-closed, shed no small amount of tears, yet said nothing at all.
Here, there is the subsiding of the transitory emotion (sañcāribhāva) called jealousy through the shedding of tears:

“When her lover, having rejected her falling at his feet, turned away from showing favor and addressed her with harsh words in anger, saying, ‘O you of silent, deceitful conduct,’ he departed; then, sighing deeply, she placed her hands upon her breasts and cast her gaze—veiled by tears of the eyes—toward her friends.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi, pha) “O you who are silent, you whose conduct is that of a rogue!
"Having said this" means [this is] the sense;
"by the proud woman with her hand placed upon her breast" is the sense;
here, there arises despondency.
“This form of the intoxicating-eyed woman, which is a delight to the pair of eyes and difficult to obtain even through the activity of the mind, gladdens my heart and yet torments me.”
Herein is the junction (*saṃdhi*) of joy and sorrow:
"Where is an improper act, and where is the lineage of the moon?
Yet she is seen once more..."
My learning is for the sake of pacifying my faults; even in anger, my face remains lovely. What will those who are stainless and wise say of me?
"She is difficult to find even in a dream; regain your composure of mind—who indeed is the fortunate youth that shall drink from her lip?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) "Where is there anything improper?"—this is the speech of Purūravas, who has desisted from the intent to die during his separation from Urvaśī.
Here, at the end of the word *kulam*, there is a deliberation (*vitarka*).
At the end of "seti," there is eagerness (*autsukya*);
at the end of "śrutam," there is discernment (*mati*) consisting of the determination of the meaning;
and at the end of "mukham," there is recollection (*smaraṇa*).
At the end of "kṛtadhiyaḥ" there is doubt;
at the end of "durlabhā" there is dejection;
at the end of "upaihi" there is fortitude.
The inquiry begins with "Who indeed," and so forth;
[it concerns] the relative strength of these transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) in comparison to each preceding one.
Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.

Herein lies the variegation (*śabalatā*) of reflection (*vitarka*), longing (*araitukya*), intelligence (*mati*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), apprehension (*śaṅkā*), dejection (*dainya*), and anxiety (*dhūti-cintā*).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Definition of Rasa and Other Elements," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
